SCDDEN DEATIL—On Friday. George Trantom, aged :16 years, of liaira-street, %Varrington, employed as a carter by Messrs. Cooper, brickrnakers, of Woolton, was engaged in loading cinders in the goods yard of Padgate Station, when he complained to a man working on a truck near, of feeling unwell and asked for a drink of water. Immediately after, however, he was seen to fall. Mr. Roberts, the stationmaster, and others were quickly in attendance, and artificial respiration was r eserted to, but they were unavailing. It is understood that the cause of death was the bursting of a blood vessel. _ •

SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO MR. JOSEPH ROBERTS.—OD Saturday evening. Mr. Joseph Roberts, landlord‘of the Farmer's Arms, F'ernhead, met with a rather serious accident. He keeps a number of fowls at the back of the premises and of late has been the victim of some robberies. In order to put a stop to them beset some alarm guns. and while examining them on Snurday in one of the henpens he unfortunately touched tho spring of one of the guns, and some cinders which had been placed over the gun were blown into his face with great force. He received rm ugly cut and is likely to lose the sight of his left eve, He is being treated at a hospital in Manchester. Air. John Gibbing. a member of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles ambulance class, rendered first aid, until the arrival of Dr. Anderson. The left eye was removed on Wednesday morning, and it is hoped that by this means the sight of the right eye may be retained.

div.head: OFFENCES IN BANKRUPTCY.
div.p: OFFENCES IN BANKRUPTCY.
Nine Charges _Against a Warrington
Auctioneer.

At the Manchester Police Court on Wednesday a case was heard by the Stipendiary Magistrates, in which Oliver Summers, described as an auctioneer and sales- man, residing at Stockton Heath, near Warrington, was charged with offences under the Debtors Act. Mr. William Cobbett who appeared on behalf of the Public Prosecutor, said the accused was formerly a boot dealer, but latterly had carried on the business of I an auctioneer in Bridge-street, NVarrington. He filed his petition on December 4 last. A number of charges were made against him.find the prosecution was founded upon an order by the County Court Judge at Warring- ton for offences under section 11 of the Debtors' Act. The offences related to the disposal of a quantity of his stock by the defendant in the latter part of the month of November, 1905, almost immediately before be filed his petition. He was accused of having con- cealed from the trustee in lannkruptcy the fact that he bad such stock; of having disposed of it, and applied the proceeds to his own purposes. It was re oposed only to take sufficient evidence to justify a remand. Detective inspector William Ashton proved the arrest of the defendant under a warrant. There were nine separate charges, end the defendant, on hearing what they were, denied that he had concealed anything or that he had sold goods, or failed to account for moneys 'received. . _ .

.„„..„ The defendant nsked for bail. Mr. Cobbett said he could not resist the application. The defendant being charged with it misdemeanour, it ss-as a reasonable one, but under all the circumstances the bail should be substantial. The defendant was remanded till Thursday next, and admitted to bail in two sureties of .£lOO each.

div.head: GERNIAN GIPSIES AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: THE GERNIAN GIPSIES AT EARLESTOWN.

On Thursday night lasta party of the German Gipsies who have given so much trouble to the police in various parts of the country, arrived in Eerlestown. and pitched their belongings on the vacant land near Heather Brae, off Market-street. Considerable attention was esoited, and on Friday morning ci ()was assembled. eyitg the strangers with idle curiosity. The eipsies did not seem at all concerned. The police under Inspector Innes, eventually cleared them out, and they resumed their wandering.

A stage coach would have been more in keeping with the antiquated cut of his clothes, his hat might have been worn by the Vicar of Wake- field, his face was in keeping with his gar- ments. It was a type of face' that has, so to speak, gone out of fashion, but which may be found still in out of the world country places. , A face round, peaceful-looking, benignant, speaking of a long life spent far from the strife i and stress of cities in some quiet village where : the stream of life passes as peaceably as the , river flowing through sunlit meadows. ! The old gentleman took a pinch of snuff from a large silver box, holding the pinch be- tween his left forefinger and thumb. He held ! out the box to Arthur with a little old- fashioned bow not wanting in a certain grace . and dignity. 1 "No, thank you," said Arthur. lake snuff; thanks all the same." 1 "It is a bad habit," said the old gentleman, i inhaling his pinch ,in a dreamy manner and re- turning the box to his pocket, but we all of us 1 —as I said only last Sunday to my flock—we : all of us, strive how we will, absorb a bad : habit or two in our passage through this most imperfect of all imperfect worlds." : Arthur was much impressed by the old man's manner and words; there was an air of benignity about him that lent a great weight to whatever he said, and they conversed on I several topics as the traie_ bore them past Ox- ford Street, Marble Arch, and Lancaster 'Gate. then down a narrow and mean-looking street. "This way," said the old man and they entered a narrow lane between two high walls, one of those numerous rights of way or short cuts that in London serve aY fobtpaths. A place to be avoided at night, a place ,that even in the day time had a desolate and sinister air. Few people passed through it and it was so narrow that two people, could not walk comfortably abreast. They h9d reached alx:tut the middle of this place when Arthur, who was walking first, suddenly received a smashing blow on the back of the head and dropped as though shot without a cry, without a 'Murmur, on the hard flags of the pavement. He had been struck with a sandbag, a weapon that knocks a man senseless yet Leaves no mark, or scarcely a bruise.

CHAPTER lIIJ " WHERE did they find him ? " "Here, right here on the pavement." "Have they gone for the ambulance ? " " Fit I should think." "Pass along, please; pass along please." Arthur Esmond heard these words spoken, he heard them vaguely as in a dream. The lane was crowded with people as far as its narrow- ness would permit, .but they seemed unreal, like people in a vision. "Feel better riow ? " asked a voice behind him, as a hand dabbed something cold on his forehead.

"Better—yes, thanks,"/ he murmured. "What has happened ? " Suddenly/as if a veil lifted, his brain cleared. He felt at his side; searched wildly for the bag and chain, then the horrible calamity came upon him in all its terror, the bag was gone 1 He struggled to his feet without a word; ' willing hands helped to hold him as he stood swaying about like a drunken man. "I- have been robbed," he said; "robbed, robbed," he could bring his tongue as yet to no more than a bald statement of the fact. The horror of the thing held his intellect as in a vice. " Robbed," said the • policeman who had been summoned. "Can you walk, sir? Well, better come and make a statement. Make room there, make room there. Did you never see a gentleman ill before? This way, sir." He supported Arthur to the opening of the stifling lane. The fresh air of the street brought new life to the runfortunate young man, and they passed through the sunlit streets and the warm summef day to the police station. Here a black-bearded sergeant of police took down a statement of the affair as far as Arthur could recollect it. He remembered everything distinctly up to the moment of entering l the narrow lane with the old gentleman; all else was blank. "You have no injury?" [asked the sergeant. "No," said Arthur. "My head is sore just here above the ear, but I don't think I am injured." "The old man with you, do you suspect him ? "

"A very lame statement," continued the manager, toying with some papers before him in a meditative manner, whilst Mr. Rob- inson, the plain clothes policeman, grunted as ,if in assent that it was a very lame statement ; so lame, in fact, as to be an absolute cripple'. "This old gentleman," said the manager, suddenly breaking Out of a reverie; " what was he like? ' " An old man, sir, dressed dike a clergy- man." "He spoke to you in the train? " " Yes, sir." " How did the conversation begin ? " He offered -me a pinch of snutl." " Did you take it ? ' " No, sir." • "What happened then? " "We had a long conversation. He told me he had not been in the city 'for fifty years. He also talked of religion and other things." " You have not been drinking, Mr. Es- mond ? " " No, sir." Arthur flushed with indignation. " Well, then, we will not trouble you with more of the conversation of this old gentle- man ; the whole thing savours of insanity. But I must point out to you that you, on urgent bank business, carrying with you close upon fifty thousand pounds' worth of 'treasure entered, according to your own confession, into a long conversation with a stranger." " But, sir—" " Not a word, please,' these are facts. It is un- pleasant, but it is a duty." " Certainly, sir," said Arthur ,Esmond, with alacrity. "Anything I can do I shall do. Even if you—if you suspect Me, have me searched now on the spot. "Well, sir," said the sergeant, " the best thing you can do is to go back to the banks If you take the tube you may reach it before closing time, and inform them of the robbery. I will telephone Scotland Yard and all the stations full particulars, and everything I will be done that can be done, It's 'a big affair, and if you will let me, I will get one of our plain clothes men to go back with you to the bank to take down particulars. In a few minutes Mr. Robinson made his appearance, a burly, stolid-looking gentle- man in a bowler hat and black cut away coat. He received his sergeant's instructions, given in a few concise words, and then they departed, the click of the telephone as they passed [the door intimating that the sergeant was ringing up Scotland Yard and that the affair was indeed "in hand."

div.head: CHAPTER 11.
div.p: CHAPTER 11.

Arthur could not help smiling, wretched though he felt, at this frank confession, and a rapid liking was growing in hini for the ill- tempered wall-eyed, lantern-jawed porter. They took an omnibus that would drop them at Gower Street, and Mr. Strathers .as he sat beside Arthur on. an outside seat. deliver. ..A himself of various opinions on the world and things in general. Arrived at Arthur's rooms in Montague Place Mr. Strathers developed a new aide to his character.

"I know you're a gentleman, Mr. Es- mond," said he, "and if so be that you'll promise me not to do anything foolish I won't trouble you with my company, but step down and make myself agreeable to your lanjiady the kitchen ; she'll give me a meal and a shake down for the night. What will she say? Leave tat to me, sir, if you'll only tell her that Prh a pore old servant of your father's who is down on his luck and wants •a lodging for the night, I'll do the rest. Then to- morrow morning we can go to the bank to- gether. What Mr. Rowlands will say to you, sir, to-morrow I don't know, neither do I know what my wife will say to me for stopping Out all night without leave. Keep up your heart, Mr. Esmond. things might be worse.. You aren't a married man." And with this cryptic pronouncement on the married sthte Mr. Strathers turned and contemplated the street whilst Arthur knocked at the door ol No. —, Montague Place.
(To .be continued.).

div.head: ATHLETES PLEASE NOTE.
div.p: ATHLETES PLEASE NOTE.

It is of interest to the modern athlete to know that the training diet of ancient times was strictly confined to only those foods which supplied abundant nourigh- meat without taxing the body. Bread, cheese, thin wine, and the small dried currants of Greece, almost made up the food of the competitor in the ancient games. The prudence of introducing currants into training dietary is obvious.

HBAT LOST BY RADIATION.

The amount of heat lost by radiation from bare pipes containing steam at 100 lb. pressure has been estimated to be about equal to' two tons of coal a year for each ten square feet of pipe surface. It has also been found that 88 per cent, of this loss can be saved by the best pipe covering.
DISAPPEARING PLANTS.

Certain flowers abroad have been lost for I nearly a century and rediscovered by chance in a different locality, thriving and abundant. In some cases the interval of time has been shorter, and, on the other hand, all of them have not beep found yet. No one knows the cause of their disappearance, by what means they were removed, or why they prefer their new habitat. One curious feature is that these vanished flowers, or shrubs, are not, as a rule, insignifi- cant plants that one might overlook- On the,' contrary, the beautiful variety of sumacis, named after Michaux, a French botanist, which was lost so many years, and has only recently - been found again, bore great panicles, or tufts, of creamy blossoms first, and later on thick. clusters of velvety and crimson fruit. Its leaves also turned a rich crimson in autumn, so that it seemed to flame and glow on the mountain sides.. Another lost plant, also a shrub, the Elliottis, was a striking beauty. It belonged to the heath family, and had long spikes of white blossoms, each blossom shaped like a St. Andrew's cross, in vivid contrast with its lustrous green foliage. It has now vanished as completely as if it had never existed. No reason is known for this low, either to botanists or the people among whom it once bloomed.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATfI GAiDEN SOCIETY.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATfI GAiDEN SOCIETY.
SECESSFUL ANNUAL 5137/. Upping By Lnly Acton.

The Stockton Heath Garden Society is only a young organization but it has already placed much useful work to its credit. The many beautiful and trimly- kept gardens, which have added so Much to the attractiveness of the village testify to the gre it intereSk _which the Society has created in matters horticultural. Still more convincing proof of the progress of the movement was afforded on Saturday when the Society held its fifth annual show in the Institute, Victoria- square. Not only was there a splendid increase in the number of entries hut a striking improvement in the quality of th, exhibits was noted. Adjoining the Institute a large marquee had been erected and this, in addition to the large room of the Institute itself, was filled with the choicest specimens of flowers, fruit and vegetables. The arrangement of the exhibits was all that could be desired and the effect Was very pleasing to the eye. A new feature of the show, and one which attracted general attraction. was the com- petition for groups of plants, eight feet in diameter, and some very fine collections were on view. The first prize went to Mr. G. Tandy who displayed a ' circular group most tastefully arranged. Palms formed the centre piece and there was a margin of beautiful carnations, lilies, ferns, and variegated vine. Mrs. Massey obtained the second award with an excellent group, including acalvpha sanderea, maiden hair fern, lilies, white hanging companulas, and a beauti- ful new variety ot verbena named "Mrs. Wilmot." Another innovation was a capital show lof hanging baskets—about sixteen in number —which were sus— pended along the centre of the tent and much enhanced ! the general effect. Mr. W. Downs was awarded the first prize. His basket hada fuchsia in the centre and ! round it were arranged geraniums, trailing companulas I and sedum. Mrs. Sampson secured the second prize with a very pretty basket with geranium as centre piece. There was an exceptionally creditable display of table decorations, the prevailing flower being the sweet pea, interspersed with gypsoplaylla. Other flowers used were "Love in a mist " (Mrs. Jelryl) and smilax. • The first prize for the best group of plantsivrent to Mr. J. Owen, and in this section colens, begonia and asparagus fern figured promi- nently. The show was remarkable for- the wealth of sweet peas sent for exhibition, and there were some lovely specimens. The winner slinived the foilowinF varieties :—" Walter P. Wright," "Prince of \Vales, ' " Hon; Mrs, Kenyon," " Dorothy. Eckford," " King Edward and " Gladys Unwm," and the second award was gained by, a collection which included the following :—" Helen Lewis," " ?iomolo Plazzana," " Bolton's pink," "John Ingman," " King Edward VII." and " Dorothy Eckford." Mr. Fred Broady won Mr. Finlayson's special prize of a silver rose bowl for the best six roses in the show, his varieties .being "Mildred Grant,' Bessie Brown," f‘ Mamie," ," Pearl von Godesbery,' "Killarney," and "Joseph Hill," all of which were hybrid tea roses, Mr. Broady alSo carried dff the first prize, in the open class for roses. The vegetable section was very satisfactory, there being some particularly good exhibits of potatoes. Mr. W. thinbridge, who won the first award for he best collection of vegetables (eight varieties) had a capital lot of potatoes, carrots, parnsips, cauliflowers, leaks, kidney beans, and peas. One box of vegetables shown by .Mr. A. B^olly secured two first prizes and a second. The following sent exhibitt not for competition : Sir Gilbert Greenall; Bart., The Mayor, Mr. Vera B. Davies, Mr. R. I. Wynne Jobes„ Mr. A. J. Willett, Mr. J Ryan, Mr. John iairhurst, Mr. E. Slater, Mr. G. Tandy,. Mr. W. Power; Mrs., Massey, Mr. Yarwood and P ferpoint and Company. Mr. Ward, of Walton, showed a hive of bees which proved an interesting feature of the show.
THE OPENING CEREMONY. SPEECH BY LADY ACTON.

There was a large attendance at the opening ceremony which was performed by Lady Acton.. Vere B. Davies, who presided, said his first duty was to offer a welcome on behalf of the Stockton Heath Garden Society to Lady Acton—(applause)—and to say how very pleased they were to see her once more in that neighbourhood. They appreciated very much her kindness in coming to their show. As regarded the Society, he hoped and trusted that it was doing a good work and he thought they might be well satisfied with the progress they had made. The Society was founded in 1902 and that was the filth show they had had. The Secretary had furnished some figures which he (Mr. Davies) thought expeesed better than anything else the advance which had been made. The number of mernbers last year was 312 ; this year it was 475—an increase of 163. Last year the inside entries •totAled 288, whereas this year they had advanced to 586; while the outside entries this year numbered 49 as compared with 16 at the last show. The figures, he thought, were conclusive evidence that the Society was in a healthy condition, and be hoped it would continue to improve. They bad made a new departure in having a show of spring bulbs and he believed it was quite a success. They hoped in future to have a show for spring bulbs in gardens and prizes would be offered. Their off-shoot—the Tree Planting Society—was also in a flourishing condition: It had a somewhat stormy and checkered youth and the speeches and hatters in the papers were, to put it mildly,ft little fiery and strong. (Laughter.) He thought now that everything was settled and there would be peace and happiness in the future. He had now pleasure in ask- ing Lady Acton to declare the show open. (Applause.) Lady Acton who was cordially received, said her gratification at having been invited to open the show was,. it possible, enhanced by the interesting statistics which, Mr. Vero Davies had just given them • for they showed how greatly the Stockton Heath Garden Society had gained, even since last year, in importance and prosperity. (Applause). When she came home in spring after a considerable absence, she was immensely strucli by-fle. improvement of Stockton Heath which, slab. understood, was owing to the movement initiated by that Society and which had led to the planting of nearly four hundred trees. At one time no doubt, the spot on which they stood really was a heath—a wild, unculti- vated tract of land, covered with moss and heather, the I haunt of birds and beasts, possibly of wilder life still in the shape of highwaymen and such like picturesque bat undesirable personages. They certainly did not want to go back to that ' state of things—(langhter)— but preferred that Stockton Heath should live up to its romantic name in another way—by blendiag the country with the town in that modern combination of the two which had so many advantages and which was generally described as the Garden City. (Applause.) There was an Eastern saying—she believed it was attributed to Mohammed—that if a man could only afford to buy bread or daffodils, he should choose the latter, because bread only fed the body whereas the beauty of flowers nourished the soul. She dld not think many of them would feel inclined to soar as high as that and fortunately on that occasion they were not driven to make the choice, for their Society seemed to cater for both the practical and the ideal sides of life, and she saw before her exhibits which provided for both ; what with splendid vege- tables, delicious looking fruit and he graceful table

div.head: SPARKS FROM GAS MANTLES.
div.p: SPARKS FROM GAS MANTLES.

The assertion that the rare earth metals of the incandescent gas-mantle emit sparks on being scratched with a file has been investigated by Baron von Welsbach. He finds that the sparks are produ&d only when the rare metals are al- loyed with 30 per cent, of iron, and he proposes to apply this property of the alloy to the auto- matic lighting of gas. As the gas is turned on, a file gently rubs the alloy, producing a brilliant shower of sparks, .which immediately ignites the gas.

The judgment of the Court THE OTHER SIDE of Appeal has prolonged the OF PASSIVE Education controversy into

RESISTANCE. the Parliamentary recess and theret is no subject at present in prospect which is likely to claim more public attention between this time and the day when the two Houses re-assemble. The judgment has created a great clash of opinions and inter- pretations. There are those who contend that it makes the new Education Bill unnecessary, which it certainly does not do, for the objection to the Act of 1902 did not rest on one ground only. That measure was objectionable because it gave away public money without establishing public control, and because, in schools maintained by this public money, it imposed sectarian tests on teachers, as well as because it endowed certain forms of religious teaching out of the rates. The new Bill is, indeed, as necessary as ever, for even if the judgment of the Court of Appeal were to be sustained by the House of Lords the condition of the Education question would still remain chaotic if it were not reduced to order by new and more dependable legislation. Lord _HUGH CECIL, who was one of the authors of the Act of 1902, now finds that measure to be flagrantly unjust because it missed out something which he and his friends intended it to include. Concerning its flagrant injustice we have no dis- pute with him. That has been our own descrip- tion of the Act froth the first. it was intended to be unjust to serve a merely Party purpose, and all that has now been discovered is that, by acci dent, it is less unjust than it was meant to be. Lord HUGH CECIL is simply in the position of the engineer hoist with his own petard. In his astonishment he proposes to adopt the weapon which has been employed by those who have objected to the measure for reasons totally different Ifrom his own. He urges Churchmen to!offer Passive Resistance to Cowper-Temple teaching. It is an astonishing battle-cry to come from such a I quarter. The doctrine of the authors of the whole Party to which they belonged, was that Passive Resistance could under no circumstances be justi- fied. Nonconformists with an objection to pay for teaching which was destined to put an end to Nonconformity were enjoined to confine themselves to purely Parliamentary action. They were assured that their proceedings were not only improper, but utterly illegal. Well, if Passive Resistance was illegal, how does a man like Lord HUGH CECIL Come to recommend it ? Is it, we wonder, to be maintained that a Churchman may steal a horse where a Nonconformist must not look over a hedge.

Lord HUGH CECIL, who is a man bf much cleverness and real distinction of character, seems to be constitutionally incapable of understanding the case of his antagonist. He assumes, for instance, that resistance to Cowper-Temple teach. ing is as easily to be justified as resistance to dogmatic teaching. The difference is, of course, that in one case Anglo-Catholicism and Roman Catholicism were forced upon the children of Non- conformist parents, and that in the other there is no teaching of the tenets of any sect whatever. It was Lord Huai CECIL himself who in- structed us on the subject of a school with two doors, one of them leading int the Estab- lished Church; and he can now, no more than then, see the difference bstween indoctrinating a child with a religion to which its parents con. scientiously object and teaching religion in a form to which, since it includes nothing of a sectarian character, cannot be open to conscientious objec- tion on any similar ground. We are glad, how- ever, that Lord Huoil CECIL has begun to look at Passive Resistance from the other side. The con- templation of it from his own point of view may at length bring him to understand that the views of others are possibly entitled to as much consideration as his own, may make him more tolerant—may impart to him that broadminded- ness which he stood so much in need of when he assisted in the passing of an enactment that he now finds to be flagrantly unjust.
HEROIC HORNSEY CITRATE.

Information has come to hand of two lives having been saved in one day by the Rev. E. Synnott, curate at St. Saviour's, Crouch Hill. Whilst at Bognor the curate heard cries of" Help," and saw a bather in diffi- culties. Flinging off his coat he planged into the sea, and though he was clutched by the throat by the drown- ing man he succeeded in bringing him safely to shore. On his return from Bognor the same day Mr. Synnott rescued another man from certain death on the rail- Way.

Humdrum and work-a-day THE CULT or THE a place as Warrington is, BEATJTIFUL. it has the redeeming feature of striving for higher things, and moreover it looks better for the effort. Nearly every village on the outskirts of the town has its flower show, and in a few weeks Warrington itself will revel in the luxury of a show all its own, where the flowers and green things will have actu- ally been grown within the shad lw of the chimneys and the smoke. This will be due to the efforts of the Beautiful Warrington Society, which bids fair in time, to transform the external appearance of the old town. Last Saturday the Stockton Heath Garden Society held its annual show, which was a credit to the village, and strong evidence of the interest taken by the " Heathens" in horticulture. An exceptionally interesting and thoughtful little speech was delivered at the opening ceremony by Lady Acton. In this age of high pressure people are too apt to become absorbed in matters utilitarian to the exclusion of everything else and her ladyship put ,1 in a powerful plea for the cult of the beautiful ' which we feel sure will further stimulate the laudable efforts of the Garden Society and kindred organisations.
Seldom has a more deter- THE SUICIDE AT mined case of suicide been LATCHFORD. recorded than the one at

L stchford on Tuesday, when a man suffering from depression, and under the influence of drink, jumped into the Ship Canal from Fairfield-road. Though he had a companion with him, he could not be prevented from carrying out his awful intention. There are some peculiar features about the case. Two other men who were passim, saw the deceased make his fatal leap, and tan with the most callous indifference they proceeded to the cantilever bridge "where they stood and watched him drown," in the words of the principal witness. It is unfortunate that their identity has not been discovered. We should like to have seen these two cowardly creatures held up to the contempt of their fellows. A young man named Bowcock why arrived on the scene very soon after the occurrence, behaved like a true Britisher. With ! the help of a rope he descended the precipitous bank, entered the water, and got the suicide to the side but he was dead. Had this young man been a few minutes earlier he would have had the gratification of seeing his pluck rewared by the saving of the victim's life. Ho is, nevertheless, deserving of warm praise for his plucky attempt at rescue. Not many young men would have ventured so unhesitatingly on such a hazardous task ! The Ship Canal is 'somewhat of a death- I trap, and there is small hope for the person who gets, intentionally or accidentally, into its deep waters. There hays been two fatalities in the canal at Latchford this surnmer,and it has occurred to many people that both lives might have been saved had there been a boat at eithei the Latch- ford or Stockton Heath Swing bridges. The Ship Canal Company should be induced to consider the advisability of taking such a precaution. The insecure protection afforded by the simple post and rail fence along the roads bordering the canal should also be seriously considered. Were the canal merely a deep pit on some open ground, the local authority would soon see that it was properly safeguarded. We think that a fence of the well- known " unclimbable " variety should be sub- stituted for the one which, at present, is no bar to either children or adults.

When a man has achieved THE VISIT OF THE such a noble work as General GENERAL, Booth he is justly entitled to the respect and admira- tion of the community. We believe we are right in saying that in the religious and social work of to-day there is no more beloved figure than the aged head of the Salvation Army. His motor campaign from Inverness to Plymouth has so far been of the nature of a triumphal progress a9d on Tuesday Warrington felt honoured in having, a visit from the General and accorded him a rousing reception. It is as remarkable as it is touching to I see this venerable leader,now in his seventy-eighth year yet full of zeal, and activity on behalf of the masses. The " Army " and its founder have had to pass through the fire of criticism but slowly a change has come over public opinion and it is generally conceded that the marvellous world-wide organization which the General has built up takes a foremost place among religious and bene- ficent agencies. As the General explained in his powerful address on Tuesday the great aim has been to reach the multitudes who are outside the scope of ordinary religious effort—the "churchless crowd." How many people have been rescued from conditions of degradation and given a new lease of life through the good offices of the Salvationists it would be impossible to estimate. Amid scenes of squalor and misery the work has been pursued and has borne its fruit in brightened homes and transformed careers. The social side of the Army's operations is indeed far reaching. Rescue homes, labour colonies, emigra- tion agencies all form part of the great scheme to help the distressed. The General has a genius for organization coupled with a deep-rooted sympathy for the poor, and it is his unconquerable zeal which stimulates his great army in their self- sacrificing labours. We are sure he would leave Warrington favourably impressed with the warmth of the greeting accorded him and, on their part, Warringtonians were delighted to hear such an interesting address from the General.
The Memorandum of the A GOOD TEIING Board of Education on FOR THE instruction in rural evening VILLAGES. classes is a document which

deserves to be widely and sympathetically studied. The authority which provides in some of our melancholy villages during the winter, education upon these lines, will be undertaking public philanthropy. Everything is to be done in relation to the ordinary occupation of the villagers. Arithmetic is to deal specifically with the economic problems thsy have to face, reading may be directed upon parish council naattors and cooperative farming, the draw- ing wnl he of sheds and chicken-house, and the carpentering is to be done according to tho drawing. Geography is to begin with the locality and to progress along unconventional lines by a consideration of railway and canal rates. The youtful and rural arithmeticians will work out the cost of fodder, tillage, and carriage, will learn the prices of materials and the administra- tion of capital,. while the Domestic Arts for young women will include,besides the making of children's clothes and the cooking of food, the keeping of domestic accounts. In the technical course, the instructor will come down to the allotment, and make the small holder an expert grower, wise in the hidden things of croppings and markets, whether the plot by which he augments his wages be garden, allotment,or small holding. Altogether, these proposals are admirable. It remains now for local residents to ascertain their representa- tive's opinions on the Memorandum.

In this month are visible THE FILLING STAR, the whole or part of the constellations designated as the Scorpion, Ophiuchus (the Serpent-bearer) with his serpent, part of Hercules ; Libra—the Scales ; Sagittarius—the Archer ; and Lupus—the Wolf. As the heavens at this time of the year are clearer than they become in November the anaateui astronomer who has a fairly good field-glass is able to identify many galaxies of luminaries which ornament the northern hemisphere. We in Europe have reason to be proud of the Great Bear. Down South the Australasians may boast of the Southern Cross. They may make it symbolical of the new British Empire which is to replace the played-out Mother Country. But the Southerners possess a sign in the heavens which is unique. It is the " S3ck of Coals.' Tnis by the black aborigine is regarded as the hole through which When a man dies his spirit goes and gets on to the roof of the world. It takes him generations before be climbs down the roof and gets back to terra firma. By that time his black skin has got perfectly white. He then reappears as a white man, having quite forgotten his former black existence. The way to get up to the hole is by a rope, which the other spirits throw down, and thsi rope is always to be seen dropping when what we call a shooting star falls.

A pathetic cry has jest gone Is ST. HELENA TO Up. It is like the cry of a BE ABANDONED? marooned mariner. St. Helena is to be abandoned It has a population of 4,000, and in a month's time there will be nobody left to preserve order in \ the white community but five coloured policemen. The Army is being withdrawn. Toe island will lie defenceless, and the Germans may swoop down upon it any dark night. It seems a desperate situation. Only the other day the children ware singing patriotic songs and saluting the flag—as happy in a full day's holiday on Empire Day as any children in the Empire could be—and uw a writer in the "Empire Review" questions,in deep dejection, whether there will be so much as a British flag left in the island next Empire Day. This looks like Napoleon's opportunity, if he should " rise from his grave," as Schubert's " Two Grenadiers "were disposed to anticipate. There are 200 English settlers on the island,and the roads and telephones have been kept up by the military. It looks as though an impetus is to be given to the cause of local self-government,and the work of the Standing, Joint Committee is, we imagine, likely to be increased. There is some talk of the white settlers leaving. Changed as their lot may be, we hope that nothing so tragic as this may follow. T'ney are holding one of the outposts of Empire. It would be a pity if there should be no one but the Africans left to ask one another " are you there ?' through the telephones and hoist the Union Jack.

At Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, the•following licensing transfers were granted : —Off licence, Chorley-street,frim Robert Whitfield to George Starkey ; off licence, 275, Knutsford-road, from John West to Peter Holt Lake ; off licence, 16 and 13, Greenall-street,from "(Lary E. Payton to John Chrim es ; Norton Arms Hotel, from executors of John .Sampson to John West ; Borough Arms, from Elizabeth Riley to Enoch A. Hollingworth. SUGAR. IS DEARER.—Advt. LAWN TENNIS, CROQUET, and other outdoor sports.—J. S. GARLAND, 51,Bridge-St.—Advt. Junior Conservative Drive. On Tuesday evening the members of the Junior Conservative Association held their second evening drive. Twenty-three buses left the club carrying about a thousand persons. There was a great demand for tickets, and a good many had to be left behind disappointed, as there was not sufficient accommoda- tion in the vehicles. The party visited Woolston, Padgate, Croft, Middleton, and Winwick. They arrived back at the club at about 10.30, the out- ing being greatly enjoyed. ' UNDER THE CLOCK for Good Bows. Advt.— J, R. Woop, Piano Dealer and Tuner, 47, Old London-road., Stockton Heath.—Advt. Camps at Prestatyn. • On Monday 140 boys left Warrington for a week's holiday at the Warrington Summer Camp at Prestatyn. They left during afternoon, and it is hoped they will spend a happy time at the seaside. The camp will break up on Saturday or Monday, when a fortnight will have been s•pent at Prestatyn by girls and a fortnight by boys.—The North-western camp of the Church Lads' Brigade has this year been held at Prestatyn, the St. Clements's and St. Elphin's Com- panies being amongst the number. On Saturday the camp broke up and the Warrington Companies arrived in Warrington about 2.30 under the command of Captain Brookes, all looking very well after their week's holiday. BACON, HAMS, AND CHEESE ARE DEARER.—Advt. PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Volunteers Return. The Warrington Volunteers returned home from camp on Saturday. For the previous fortnight the men had been under canvas on Salisbury Plain,where they formed part of the 30th Field Army Brigade. Throughout they have acquitted themsevles in a , manner which reflected the greatest credit on the corps. The men, travelling by three special trains, arrived at Warrington between 5.30 and 7 p.m. They looked bronzed and it was evident that they had ' benefited greatly by the fortnight's fresh air and exercise. Largo crowds met them at the station and hundreds followed them to the Drill Hall where the men were dismissed. The fatigue party, under the direction of Captain and Quarter-master Potter, returned to the Drill Hall at eight o'clock on Monday evening. The men looked remarkably well. PREMIER CYCLES, 7,8, 10, 12 and 14 guineas Cash or IS monthly pyyments. Sole agent, J.S. GARLAND, 51, 53 and 55, Bridge-st.—Advt. Fires at Warrington. At about ten o'clock on Sunday morning, informa- tion was received at the Fire Station that a fire had broken out in the warehouse at the rear of Mr. W. Isaac's premises in Buttermarket-street. The brigade under the direction of Superintendent Turner,promptly turned out with reel, ladders and the steam engine, Captain." On arrival they quickly got a hydrant to work from Buttermark-et-street, and the fire which was confined to the basement was soon extinguished. The little damage done,is covered by insurance.—At about 10.30, on Monday morning, a fire broke out at Parr Hall. The fire brigade turned out in charge of Superintendent Turner, and on arrival they found that Mr. Powys,the caretaker had got to work with the Hall appliances. His efforts were supplemented by the brigade and the flames were soon extinguished. The damage is small. _

Mr. Coroner Brighouse, held an inquest at the Police Station on the body of James Atherton, aged 62, carter, who resided with• his son Zachariah Atherton, tailor, 11, Miller-street. On Tuesday after- noon, August 7th, Atherton was seen by Charles Gatley, weir attendant at Howley, to take off his jacket and cap, and jump into the river Mersey. G-atley.at once got a boat, and with great difficulty taken to the Workhouse
I rescued Athert. He was t.. Hospital, in a collapsed _ _

_ , - - state. He devolopsd pneumonia, and died On Saturday. Deceased's son said his father had for the past three years suffered from softening of the brain, but, to his knowledge. had never threatened to take away his life.—Dr. Braide expressed the opinion that had it not been for the immersion deceased would not have had pneumonia.—The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst of unsound mind." THE "WARRINGTON FOOTBALL ANNUAL AND SPORTS RECORD."—On Sale, Saturday, August 25th, —will contain 70 pages of information indispensable to all local sportsmen. Sad Drowning Fatality. Mr. H. Dobson conducted an inquest, at the Stag Inn, Lower Walton, on Tuesday, on the body of Herbert Barnes, aged seven years, 27, Erwood-street, Warrington, who was drowned whilst bathing in the Old Quay Canal at Lower Walton, the previous after- noon. Frederick Shelmerdine, aged eight years, stated that be, the deceased, and two other boys went a walk along the river side, and when they came to the Old Quay Canal at ' Walton the decease commenced to bathe. He had been bathing about .half-an-hour when he suddenly sank.—Henry Charles Prother, employed by the Ship Canal Comyany at the Stag Bridge, stated that at 4.45 on Monday afternoon, a little boy came and told him that a lad had been drowned near the Twelve Arches. He proceeded there and with the assistance of Sergeant Kennerley succeeded in recover- ing the body with grappling irons and a boathook. The boy had'sunk in a hole which was about seven feet deep,—A verdict of " Accidentally drowned " was returned.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE AND LABOUR PARTY.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE AND LABOUR PARTY.
MEd

The local members of the Independent Labour Party at Widnes are apparently still determined to persevere with their struggle for freedom to hold open-air meet- ings. They were disappointed on Saturday by the non-arrival of their speaker from Glasgow, consequently their meeting at the Big Lamp was abandoned. On Sunday afternoon the weather was so unpropitious that only a few congregated around to hear Ur. Kilday give an address, so that the police kept away, doubtless because they thought no obstruction was being caused. In the evening Mr. Kilday addressed a meeting of greater dimensions, and whilst the speaker was dealing with social questions generally the police, under their new Inspector (Mr. Tongue) arrived upon the scene. —Mr. Kilday was asked to move on, but stoutly refused.—lnspector : I ask you to move on for a second time.—Mr. Kilday : I shall not move away.—lnspector Tongue : Then give me your name and address.—Mr. Kilday readily gave his address-84, Roxburgh-street, Greenock, after which about ten policemen and sergeants dispersed the crowd, and kept them all a good distance away from the speaker, who could only be heard by the reporters.—Addressing the police, Mr. Kilday said they would have a good ride to bring him. When they got to his home, his old mother would make them a cup of tea or coffee,or give them some "beans."— Rain commenced to fall, and after a collection had been taken amongst the scattered audience, Mr. Kilday closed the meeting, and invited as many as could attend to go to the Labour Rooms, where he could resume his address. —This is the first time that the police have dispersed a meeting.

MEAN THEFTS FROM A'I3IRMAID. Peter Bowden, carter, of 89, Eccleston-street, and Margaret Ann, his wife, were charged at St. Helens on Saturday, with stealing articles of wearing apparel and jewellery.—The evidence was that Miss Naylor, formerly a barmaid at the Turks Hotel, Knotty Ash, entrusted her box to Bowden to bring to St. Helens on his lorry on June 20.—Prosecutrix went to live at Martinscsoft, near Warrington, and on making inquiries she found that her box had been taken to Bowden's house, and learned that the things had been removed. The police were informed, and Detective Roe found that Mrs. Bowden had pledged a large number of articles in various parts of the town, and sixty-nine pawntickets were found in the house. A scent bottle and jewellery and other articles were found in the child's cradle. Inspector Dunn also found a letter which the woman had written to her mother at Westhoughton, telling her that the police would be making inquiries about the goods out of the box, and she had to make certain statements, the letter ending, " Be sure and be ready for him, and try to screen me. I do not know how I shall go on, and I am very near math" The woman was arrested before she had time to sand the letter.—Bowdon declared that he knew nothing at all about the theft, and his wife supported the statement.—The magistrates discharged Bowdon,and cautioned h:ra as to his future conduct. Mrs. Bowden was dealt with leniently on account of her young baby and family, and sentenced to a month.
[BY W. R. LESTER, M.A.] Ex-President for the Scottish League for the Taxation of Land Values). 111.—IS SOCIALISNI THE REMEDY.

Starting from the premise that the earth is for the equal use of all men in all generations, and not for some men only, and that our denial of this equal right is the root cause of the distress existing in all civilised countries, we have now to inquire how far the actual legislative proposals of Socialism can either prevent or cure the evil. The Social Democratic Federation stat2s its objects to be—" The Socialisation of the means of production, distribution, and exchange, to be controlled by a democractic State in the interests of the entire community." The Joint Committee of Socialist Associations in England declares its aims to be "to obtain for the whole community complete ownership and control of the means of transport, the means of manufacture, the mines, and the land." Mr. Sidney Webb declares that the main principle of reform must be" the substitution of collective ownership and control for individual private property in the means of production." The Fabian Society is pledged to " the abolition of industrial competition." Mr. Robert Blatchford, in "Britain for the British," states the principle of Socialism to be —" That the land and all the machines, tools, and buildings used in making needful things together with all the canals, rivers, roads, railways, ships, and trains used in moving, sharing (distributing), needful things, and all the shops,markets,scalts,weights, and money used in selling or dividing needful things shall be the property of (belong to) the whole people (the nation),', and that " they shall be worked,managed, eivided, and used by the whole people in such a way as the greater number of the whole people shall deem best." It will thus be seen that under Socialism a vast central organisation called the State is to be estab- lished, which is to control and divide practically all that men do and need. In fact, that all businesses and enterprises are to be in the hands of the State. In- dividual enterprise and competition bein. regarded as hurtful things, are to be destroyed, aneState owner- ship and management substituted. Now it is not needful here to discuss whether it is humanly possible for the State as an entity to organise industry better or more purely than it is now organised, seeing that the Socialistic State would be only com- posed of individuals no better in their capacity of State officials than in their individual capacity. Nor need we consider the possibilities of corruption and favouritism under a vast single central body such as it is proposed to establish. Some may hold that the spur of competition being removed there would remain no effective substitute ; that as a result of its removal the whole race would deteriorate because individuals would be liable to have the products of their industry taken from them and divided as the majority saw fit ; that the main incentive to effort would thereby bo destroyed; that if the full reward of their work instead of being secured to each were taken from the more sapable members of the community and given to the less capable, the effect would be discouragement of , capacity, and by Darwin's law of natural selection and the survival of the fittest the tendency would be towards the non-production of capable people, which would moan a setback in the development of the race. It may be held that Socialism means interferences with the law that it is good for every ably adult to reap the consequences of his own act. Whatever may be said for or against such opinions. one certainty remains, viz. :--That only in so far as Socialism would break down existing monopoly and secure to all an equal right in Nature's bounties would it accomplish anything effective, and similarly that all time and effort devoted to the minor reforms aimed at by Socialists is time and effort wasted because such reforms could effect nothing lasting in face of the existing monopoly in Nature herself. No sooner had the gain from these minor reforms become general than it would be swallowed up in increased rent-charges on the part of the monopolists. Socialists aim, and aim rightly, at increasing the well-being of the worker ; what we have to determine is whether this can possibly be permanently attained so long as land remains private property. Take an instance of what we,mean. When Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman was at the War Office he gave a general rise in wage to the men employed in Woolwich Arsenal. Now, Woolwich is an exceptionally favourable place for tracing the effects of any economic change of this nature, because most of the workers there are employed in the Arsenal. Mark the effect of the general rise in wages. It was to cause an increase in the ground rental of Woolwich. This increased ground rent, of course, expressed itself in house rent. Where, then, did the worker profit ? lu effect, the British tax-payer who gave the rise in wage was really enriching quite a different class—the landowners. _ . .

Again, Mr. Goschen stated in the House of Commons, April 14th, 1899, that "If it were consistent with proper administrative principles to make an advance in the wages of the labourers at Deptford Victualling Yard he would cheerfully do so, but that in Woolwich and Deptford wages had been raised 20 per cent, in the last ten years, and the rents 50 per cent. It was con- stantly the case in these districts that the increase in wages resulted in a larger sum going into the pockets -of the landlords." Fair samples of the definite constructive proposals of Socialism are : (1) The providing of work for the unemployed by a charge on the rates. (2) The providing of houses for the working classes by the State or municipality. (3) The free feeding of school children. (4) A stiffly graduated Income Tax. None of these proposals touch the botto n. Take the first. It is quite certain that work in the aggregate cannot be increased by any such machinery. It only means that the ratepayers are to be called on to con- tribute o a central fund, and that this central fund is to be drawn on to pay wages to unemployed men. In other words the individual ratepayers are to be forced to surrender part of their power of demanding labour, and in their place the municipality is to acquire the power of demanding the labour. The sum of demand will not be increased one iota. Simply the individual ratepayer will be able to demand less labour, and the municipality proportionately more than now. In essence this is no more than a form of com- pulsory charity, and charity can accomplish nothing in this sense. What these unemployed men need is justice. If there is no one who wants their labonr,what is it that prevents them working for themselves ? That is what we have to find out. Then take the proposal as to housing. The munici- pality is to provide houses—if necessary at under cost. It is not enquired why these people cannot provide decent houses for themselves. This, at bottom, is but another form of compulsory charity, and will not solve the housing problem. Suppose the municipality demolishes a slum in order to provide decant houses. In the first place, under present conditions, the munici- pality is bled in the price it has to pay for the slum and its site. Outrageous sums are commonly asked for slum properties when it is known that the municipality is in the market, and in this way the ratepayers are mulcted' But suppose the one-sided bargain mada, the slum property demolished, and new houses built. What becomes of the former overcrowded inhabitants ? The common experience has been that they go oil to some other quarter there to form a new slum district. The fact is, it is only one phase of the problem of poverty. Wages are too low to pay for reasonably good accom- modation and so slum properties come into existence. Then further, what effect must build- ing by the municipality have on building in general ? Clearly, if the town builds houses under cost, private builders cannot compete; for private builders only build so long as it is profitable to do so. As it is not proposed that all the building of the town shall be done by the municipality, it follows that the result may well turn out to be less building on the whole, and dearer houses than before, because houses will be scarcer—the very opposite to what was intended. Then consider the free feeding of school children. Once more it is not enquired why the children's parents are too poor to feed them. We may feel the deepest sympathy for these poor children, and still see where such a proposal would logically land us, simply because it approaches the problem from the wrong end. Free education was the first step. Free feeding is to be the second. Then why should tot free clothing, housing and complete maintenance be the next, so relieving the parents of all responsibility for their children whatever. But suppose all this was done ; mark the economic effect under present conditions of monopoly. The relief of parents from expense in keep- ing their children is equivalent to a rise in wage, and we have already seen how that inevitably means a rise in rent, because of the increased competition for accom- modation as soon as the rise becomes general in a dis- trict. Southwark is a case in point. Hear the testi- mony of a member of a university settlement in South London. " &bout £350 is given away each year in doles of bread in connection with Christ Church, Southwark. As a consequence the competition for small houses, hut more particularly for single rooms in tenement houses in this parish, is so great that rents are considerably higher than in the neighbouring districts. And yet the clergy go on contentedly putting more than .£356 yearly into the pockets of owners of this kind of property, and call it charity.' What are we to say of proposal No. 4, for a stiffly- , graduated income tax ? The purpose is to destroy large incomes, but a most unscientific method it is. If large incomes are bad we ought to prevent their accumulation, net take them after the damage wrought by their accumulation has been done. This is like locking the stable door after the steed is gone. Either a man has earned his income or he has not earned it. If he has earqpd it, then it is rightfully his own, what- ever its amotAt, and we have no business to take it from him by taxation. If on the other hand he has not earned it, then as a sensible community, we ought to find out which of our institutions enables any man to live on the earnings of others and this ascertained, we should abolish such institution. No man ,could then have an income unless it were earned and the notion of taxing wealth by means of a graduated income income tax would only

MR. SEDDON, M.P. ON LABOUR TOPICS.

The Amalgamated Society of Paper Stainers visited Southport on Saturday. They saw the sights of the town and had tea at the Zoo Park. Mr. Seddon, the Labour member for Newton-le-Willows, accompanied the party and made a speech after tea. He emphasised the necessity for combination amongst workers, and held that under existing conditions the introduction of labour-saving machines was a curse. used for the enrichment of the employer at the expense and degrada- tion of the workers. There ought to be a further reduction of the hours of lahpur.

BUEITONWOOD COLLIER AND HIS CONCERTINA Austin Johnson, of 26, Fairclough-street, Burtonwood, a young collier, was charged at St. Helens on Monday with fraudulently converting to his own use, and thereby stealing, an English concertina.—Mr. IV. Hutchens prosecuted for Mr. Peters, Holt-street, who said that this man had a concertina, valued at 0, on the hire system, and still owed El Ss. They could get neither the instrument nor the money.—After the evidence had been given the Chairman asked for a proof of fraudulent conversion.Mr.Hutchens said he thought that the evidence was strong enLugh.—There Chairman said that there was no evidence of fraudulent conversion. The man simply refused to show the concertina to Mr. Peters, and they would have to dismiss the case.

SEQUEL TO A STRIKE. At Newton Petty Sessions on Thursday Martin Daly, of 26, Hotel-street, Earlestown, was summoned for having used abusive language to Emily Howarth, on the night of July 21st.—Nfr. Knowles, prosecuting, said Messrs. Tootal Broadhurst & Co., proprietors of a weaving mill at Bolton, had a strike among their work- people, and employed 20 or 30 Earlestown girls to take the places of strikers, paying them wages and railway fare. There were sympathizers with the strikers, it seemed, in Earlestown and Daly, that Saturday night, appeared to be remonstrating with 111 r. Owen, the I owner of some house property in Hotel-street, for letting "-- knobsticks live in his houses." He added "Here comes one !" just as the plaintiff was passing with some chips which she was fetching from a shop at the corner. She said she would make him pay for saying that. The result was that a crowd assembled, there was a disturbance, and the ' plaintiff fainted and was ill after it, and under Dr. Mouncey's care for some days.—Emily Howarth gave evidence in accord with her counsel's statement : I was in bed a week after it. I was afraid and am afraid now to go home at the week-end. My sister was thrashed by the same crowd. I did not see that; I was ill.—Mrs. B. Parkin, of 28, Hotel street, next door to the defen- dant, said plaintiff made the bother, and threw herself on the ground in temper—not a faint. Witness had known Daly 15 years and had never heard him swear.— The Bench dismissed the case, the Chairman saying there was not sufficint evidence for a conviction, but defendant made rather an indiscreet remark and ought to be a little more careful, A COLLIER WHO DID NOT" PLAY THE GAME.' A case of much interest to colliers was heard at Newton last Thursday when Joseph Sharrock was charged with stealing a pitman's tally, on the 15th July, in the Princess Pit, Haydock.—Mr. Allen, of Wigan, prosecuted, and Mr. Johnson defended.—Mr. Allen said this was one of those very rare cases in which one collier was charged with attempting to defraud others by changing the tub tallies in the pit. I This man worked with or near two others named Greenall and Southern, Greenall's tally number was 25 and Southern's 76. Tney suspected that their tallies had been tampered with, and they put private marks on their boxes, Greeaall making a small cypher and Southern a small figure 3. After they had been work- ing on Sunday night, they had,early next morning, filled letubs each, and there was an additional identification mark on one of the tubs as it had been broken at one part. On that particular tub afterwards, Sharrock's tally was found. A charge of this kind was very seldom brought, because he (Mr. Allen) was glad to say that as a rule colliers 'played the game." If necessary it could be proved that this man Skarrock stole more than one, but one was enough for this case. Anyone doing it drew the money another man ought to draw, and it was a worse offence than going to a man's house after he had taken his wages home, and taking the money out of a chest of drawers, there, because it was likely to arouse suspicion against others—perhaps the checkweightnan. It was a difficult thing to detect, but in this case the man was taxed with it in the presence of other persons, and being accused of stealing 13 tallies, he said he only had taken two. That was a sufficient admission. He asked the manager to deductl the extra money from his next week's wages. After that, how he could come to court and plead not guilty, he (Mr. Allen) could not understand. John William Greenall then deposed to the circumstances as opened by Mr. Allen, Southern, Sharrock and himself having filled ten tubs each that night. On the broken tub instead of Southern's number 70, he found Sharrock's GI. William Edward, manager at the Princess Pit, said Sharrock was questioned about the affair in presence of several witnesses. He at first said he had done nothing. Witness said "Now, Joe, you know you have done some- thing." He said" Then take it out of my money, and I'll apologise." This being the first case of the kind witness had known, he did not know what to do with it, so he sent for ex-constable Addison, and Sharrock confessed to him that he had taken two tallies. Defen- dant was sworn and said he had been working in that pit about a month, and previously had had 34 years' regular emplovnent at the Pemberton Colliery. On that Monday morning the boxes ran off the roads tally came out, and he could nct find it. He reported it to the lusher-on, not knowing whether it was one of his boxes or not. He had filled 11 tubs up to the last minute he worked. The Bench fined him 20s, and costs.
CHARGE GF SHOOTING A HONIING PIGEON.

_ ... Last Thursday at Newton Petty Sessions, Charles Baxter was charged with shooting a pigeon belonging to James Davies, on July '2lst.—Mr. H. J. Longton prosecuted for the Horning Union and Mr. Knowles defended.—Mr. Longton said his client lived in Alma- street, Earlestown, and in company with a young man named Glynn took three pigeons to the canal bank, near the Nine Arches. The defendant was employed by Mr. Bridge on his farm between the Vulcan boundary and the Nine Arches. Several owners of pigeons had complained of ther homing birds. being killed on that farm, where it was rather difficult to see who shot them. The plaintiff tossed a young bird which he was training, and it started to fly home to its loft at Earlestown. As it passed over a plantation it was shot, Plaintiff ran up the Canal bank and called to the defendant who was on the other side of the Canal, telling him he had seen him shoot. He was then in the act of aiming at thip other two pigeons.l He had since tried to settle the matter for £2., but the Homing Union instructed him (Mr. Longton) to go on with the case for the protection of pigeon owners. The value of such a bird when shot might be Gd. to the person who shot it, though homing fanciers might spend pounds on them. James Davies, crane driver at Vulcan b'oundry, gave evidence similar to Mr. Longton's opening, and said he went to Mr. Bridge's farm to find out about it, and I charged Baxter with having shot the pigeon, which he valued at 30s.—John AlcUlynn corroborated Davis's evidence, and said he went to see the defendant. Mr. Knowles, for the defence, said the pigeon might be living still for anything proved to the contrary. People out shooting raust not fire a gun now-a-days if there were pigeons flying about. If they did,the owners went home to see if their young sqneakers had got back to their •lofts. If the birds had not got home, then the owners went back to collar someone smaller than themselves and accuse him of killing a pigeon which for anything they knew might have been caught by a cat. If Mr. Bridge had not been away at Warrington perhaps he might have been summoned in this case.— Mr. Longton : You are misrepresenting the facts. Mr. Knowles: Upon my word, my friend provokes me to say these pigeon fanciers should adopt the French suggestion of crossing the pigeons with parrots, so that when they get lost they could ask the way home.— Defendant was then sworn and deposed that he did his work for Mr. Bridge that afternoon. He had no gun. He had never fired one in his life. They often heard shooting going on about there.—Winifred Willis, Mr. Bridge's servant, said she told plaintiff her master was not at home, and that there was only one gun, which had not been out of the house. Baxter had not been in the kitchen, nor had he had the gun. He would be down the yard with the cows about the time named.— The Bench dismissed the summons.

aise a smile, for all would see that instead of taxing men on their incomes we ought to encourage them to earn as much as possible. The true line of action is to tax out of existence monopoly which implies the power to live on the exertions of others. Then let all go ahead secure in the knowledge that nothing will be taken from them, whatever their incomes. The errors and miscarriages of Socialism come from treating competition and capital in private hands as being in themselves evils by their very nature. This too often leads Socialists into the barren enterprise of dealing with symptoms instead of with causes, and explains why we find them making indiscriminate attack on all kinds of men and institutions, thus misdirecting a vast amount of well-intentioned effort which if only i concentrated on fundamentals would carry ns far. When , their theories are embodied in definite legislative pro- posals we find them demanding a compulsory eight hours day, a legal minimum wage, municipal workshops 1 for the unemployed, the nationalisation of railways, ; compulsory early closing of shops, old-age pensions,free ' feeding of school children, &c. All such measures, howeveremuch present conditions I may force them on us, are the merest tinkering with , symptoms in view of the initial wrong which causes i poverty amid wealth. It is poverty, and the helpless- ness of the many to defend themselves, which causes the demand for these measures, add we have shown that , the main cause of poverty is that all the opportunities , for labour are privately appropriated and only allowed , to be used on the private owners' terms. Competition 1 under such conditions of monopoly necessarily becomes 1 one-sided. It becomes a competition for work among the disinherited because they are unable to work freely for themselves or in co-operation with others. i being denied this elementary right, most men are : driven to compete with each other for hired employ- ment, and in the absence of any alternative of self- i employment, this competition drives the wage they can command down towards subsistence. But for this we I must not blame competition itself. To do so, as i Socialism does, is to be guilty of drawing conclusions 1 from mere appearances. The present articlicial condi- tion of monopoly which blocks all avenues to employ- i ment, rends rs work scarce and competition one-sided I is, in reality, responsible for present conditions. What ! kind of competition is that which drives producers to i accept a mere subsistence, whatever may be the value i of their services, while it enables others to c ntrol the ; source of all production so that while per ming na service they become rich ? Socialists mis., ke it for 1 ft competition, though it is the very denial of equality of I opportunity, and equality of, opportunity is the essence of true competition. Competition in itself is the bugbear of Socialism wit hout any qualification as to the kind of competition. As well might the man struck by a stone blame the stone instead of thrower. What is overlooked is that given equality of opportunity, competition is the best thing for all. To condemn competition as such is not radical enough. It does not go to the root of matters. It savours too much of what is called in the States "talking in your hat." First remove the present mono- poly in natural resources, and competition instead of being the scourge it now is, yould assume its true and beneficial function of securing to each all he contri- butes to production, because it would be free competi- tion on equal terms for all. This truth was clearly seen in the imaginary case of the well, and is equally true in society as we find it to-day. Monopoly, not competition, 111119 L be the object of attack if anything at all is to be attained.

Monopoly is the antithesis of competition, and it is because of the former that true competition does not and cannot exist to-day. The distorted form of present day competition,which Socialists mistake for true com- petition, is a branch, not the tree of evil, and when the trunk of monopoly falls, one-sided, distorted competi- tion will fall with it. Far be it from us to confute the proposals of Socialism without having anything to put in their place. The most optimistic cannot view with satisfaction existing social conditions, and if cast-iron Socialism were the only alternative we would gladly accept it. Our contention is that there is a cure, but that it is not Socialisrn.ln essence Socialistic measures are protective. They aim at protecting the worker against unjust social conditions. They ought to aim at freeing the worker so that he can protect himself. There is no need for all the new laws which Socialism demands. What we really need is abolition of existing bad laws which deprive men of their freedom—which rob them of their patrimony. Men are to day made poor by law. Our first duty therefore, is to abolish present bad laws —not to enact new ones. The analysis of Socialism not being radical, its remedies must perforce hkve the same defect. Our task is to show the remedy which touches the heart of th
(To be continued).

Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. There was a good attendance at the meeting of this society in the Winwick-streot Co-operative Bali on Sunday, when the Hon. Sec. (Mr. B. Farrar) presided and expressed the thanks of Mr. Brown and Mr. Tilling for the vote of sympathy sent them in their long affliction, and of Mr. Parker for the condolence of the society in) the loss of his brother. The chairman proposed a vote of condolence with the widow of Mr. J. Riley who was killed at Manchester, by an express from Liverpool to Manchester on Thursday, last week. Mr. Riley was an , old member of the P.S.A., and a member of the coin- mittee for some years. Mr. E. A. Pickering. of Liverpool, gave an address on "The worries of life." ' Some people, he said, would worry, and try to carry the burdens of others. There were the worries of the head, also of the heart, and both were sufficient to greatly shorten the life. "Take no thought for the morrow," could be carried to extremes,but they could give reason- able thought, and give more attention to the duties of life, with as little worry as possible. Then life would be lengthened, and God's will more completely done. Mr. C. Cotton read the lesson. Miss Fairhurst sang with good effect, " Nearer to Thee." and "lie was dispised." Mr. W. H. Payton, Muo. Bac., presided at the piano. The contribution to the Organ Fund, was ..L2l 10s. Twenty-eight members joined the savings club and about £4 was deposited.

div.head: LETTER FROM MR. A. ;1. CROSFIELO, M.P.
div.p: LETTER FROM MR. A. ;1. CROSFIELO, M.P.
The following letter was sent to the Mayor by the Borough Member in connoclion with the General's visit :

Dear Mr. Mayor,—l am just leaving London this evening for Dover en 2 Oitte for Switzerland. After a. very busy time here I need a holiday, but I very greatly regret that ray absence abroad will prevent me accepting your kind invitation for the 14th. lam exceedingly sorry to miss hearing General Booth speak to us in Warrington. For many years I have profoundly respected, admired and sympathised with the work of the Salvation Army, and in a small way tried to sup- port it. It is a great disappointment to me that shall be unable to participate in the heartfelt welcome which Warrington I know on Tuesday will give the truly great man who in our generation is foremost amongst those who have helped to bring about in pre- sent and future times the regeneration of suffer- ing humanity. Believe me, dear Mr. Mayor, with thanks for your invitation, and many regrets that I cannot be in Warrington on Tuesday.—Very faithfully yours, A. H. CROSPIELD. London, August 12th,1906.

The suggestion has been made to the Manchester Guardians by the Local Government Board inspector, that the children at the Swinton schools should be allowed to camp out for a few weeks, to allow of the school buildings being thoroughly aired and disinfected

Something Like an Eel. Whilst fishing in the Bridgewater Canal at Thelwall, on Saturday, Mr. William Bancroft, of Egerton-street, Warrington, succeeded in catching an eel which weighed 211). 1330 z. The fish measured in lenth 361 inches, whilst in circumference it was seven inches, Mr. Bancroft had the greatest difficulty in securing his prize with. an ordinary rod and line. In all i probability it ill be placed in the Museum.
