div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
DRUNRES DRIVER'S FREAK.

At the Warrington Police Court on Monday. Arthur Heesom, 17,3. Knntsford-road. was charged with being drunk and disorderly in charge of a horse and trap in Knutsford-read on the sth Augnst.—He pleaded guilty. It appears that the defendant as seated on the near seat of ths trap with his beck to the horse, and was attewiting to drive in that direction, with the result that the horse was careering all over the roadway. He was fined 10s.

div.head: THEFT OF FowEs AT BURTONWOOD.
div.p: THEFT OF FowEs AT BURTONWOOD.

At the -Warrington Occasional Court, on Monday, before Mr. F. A. Frost, Henry Ellison, Lovely-lane, and Joseph Blease. 10, Dale-street, were charged with breaking and entering a hen cote at Bewsey Old Hall Farm- between 8.90 p.m. on Saturday, and 8 a.m. on Sunday, and stealing three buff Orpington pullets. valued at 305., the property of Messrs. Hatton and Reid, and a black Nfinorca cock, valued at £5. the property. of the Rev. W. Bracecamp.—Mr. Reid. who is in partnership with Mr. Hatton at Bewsey Old Hall Farm, said that he locked the hen cote up on Saturda7 night at 8.30, and it then contained 19 pnliets and a black Minorca cock-. On Sunday morning he found the door of the cote had been prized open, and parts of the fencing broken. He discovered three pullets and the black Minorca cock were missing. The latter was a show bird.—Prisoners were committed to the County Petty Sessions.—At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday Blease was fined 405.. and costs or one month's imprisonment. Ellison. who was represented by Mr. T. S. Steel, was discharged there being no evidence against him.

div.head: SUNDAY _NIGHT SCENE.
div.p: SUNDAY _NIGHT SCENE.

At the Warrin-gt-o-n—i;olic-e-.64;11-W-On-Nfonday Arthur Westwell. 12 Chester-street, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, with assaulting P. O. Fish, and also with assaulting James Sunter.—P.C. Fish stated that on Sunday night, about eleven o'clock, he was in Sankey-street when he heard a disturbance taking place in the direction of Garven House. This it transpired was created by the prisoner. The man was cautioned but as he subsequently reneated his conduct he was arrested. On the way to the police station prisoner became violent and struck witness in the face.—James Sinter stated that he was with the prisoner when they had a little argurrilnt. Prisoner knocked him down and kiaked him in the face.—Prisoner denied that he kicked Sunter. He only hit him with his fist.—A fine of 10s. and costs or 14 days was inflicted.
HEA.VY FINE AGAINST A WARRINGTON ICE-CREAM VENDOR.

_ At Newton-le-Willows on Itonday. 'Mohan Dilarauzi ice-cream vendor, of Dial-street. Warrington, appeared in the dock on a charge of cruelty to a horse. Police- constable Benson stopped the horse in Church-streat. Newton-le-Willows. on Saturday afternoon, and found it saff.rinz from a large suppurating wound, about the size of a man's hand, on the back. The backbone could be seen through the wound."-Inspector innes described it as a horrible case of cruelty. Inspector Casey. of the Revel Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, corroborated.—Defendant assenting to have the horse destroyed. the Chairman said they would have sent prisoner to gaol withont the option of a tine had he not consented. Pie was fined .£3 end costs„ or six weeks in default. The amount was £3 lEis.

div.head: SW ART SENTENCE F3E. UNPROVOKED ASSAULT.
div.p: SW ART SENTENCE F3E. UNPROVOKED ASSAULT.

At the Wirrington Police Court, on Monday, James Geraghty, 7, Sparling-street, was charged with assault- ing Annie Bowcook, wife of George Bowcock, 17, Stafford-road. on Sunday Wght. It appears that on Sunday Mrs. Bowcock visited some friends in Warring- ton, and returned home about ten o'clock. She was jest about to open the back gate when the prisoner, whom she did not know, came up and caught hold of her. She struggled and managed to get away, but prisoner again seized her and threw her down. She screaniecl and her son came out. Prisoner made off but was caught by n Mr. Plinston, who held him mail the police appeared on the scene, when he was given into costody.—Prisoner, who had nothing to say, was com- mitted to gaol for two months with hard labour.— Plinaton was thanked by the magistrates and the police for his assistance.

div.head: DISTURBERS OF VIE PEACE.
div.p: DISTURBERS OF VIE PEACE.

A somewhat rowdy scene was witnessed in Robson- street at midnight on the 4th inst. It appeared that William Dunbobbin, who was under the influence of drink, took it into his head to entertain the neighbours to selections on the cornet, ranging from "The Old Ball and Bush " to " My Irish Molly, 0." much to their annoyance. The police interfered, but retreating to his domicile and retorting that a man's house was his castle, he continued until he tired of his amusement. A neighbour. Thomas Broady, remonstrated with him, and Harry Dunbobbin taking his father's part, a fight ensued.—At the Warrington Police Court on Monday Dunhobbin, who pleaded that he was playing hymns,was tined 55. and costs (19s. in all), whilst his son and Broady were each fined ss.

div.head: ADULTERATED COFFEE.
div.p: ADULTERATED COFFEE.

At the Daresbury Petty Sessions, at Stockton Heath, I on Tuesday, Thomas Dleave, Appleton. was summoned for selling coffee which was adulterated by the addition I of 45 per cent of chicory.—Mr. Jeffs, assistant inspector of weights and measures sooke to purchasing a quarter I of a ponnd of coffee from the defendants wife.—Mr. Browne said the defendants business in coffee was chiefly in small cannisters. He however, had two nounds of a mixture of coffee and chicory Loose in a bag, to which was affixed a label stating that the article was sold as a mixture of coffee and chicory. Mrs. Gleave, however, neglected to show the label to the inspector and also neglected to affis a similar hut smaller label to the coffee which she sold though she bad a stock of labels for this purpose.—A fine of 103. was inflicted.
rOTORISTS FINED., EXCE•sSIVE SPEED ON CHESHIRE ROADS.

The county police in the neighbourhood of Warring- ton keep a vigilant watch for motorists who after leaving the borough like to indulge in a little speed work along the country roads. A much frequented road is that which runs in the direction of Chester and a police trap in July resulted in the capture of two offenders. The trap is worked by the posting of two constables one at Walton and the other at Preston Brook a distance of three and a quarter miles away. Their watches are compared before end after they go on duty and the exact moment of the passin.g of every motor car is recorded on a special card. These cards are then compared and a little mathematical calcula- tion gives the exact speed at which every car covers the three miles. The two motorists to he caught in July were Captain P. N. Avery and 3,1 r. Wm. Gossage, who covered the distance respectively at, 2G miles an hour and 27 miles an hour.—At the Daresbery Petty Sessions on Tuesday both were anedl4os. and costs.

div.head: WARRINGTON HUSBAND'S SHOCKING CONDUCT.
div.p: WARRINGTON HUSBAND'S SHOCKING CONDUCT.

William Hewitt. a tanner, living at 11, Albert-terrace, was summoned at Warrington Courtl on Tuesday morn- ing, to show cause why a separation order should not be granted to his wife on the ground that he was an habitual drunkard. Tle was also charged with having been drunk and disorderly. Mr. Steel appeared for the complainant, and said the prisoner was the man who

made himself notorious some time ago by jumping into the Mersey, but he took care not to drown himself. He appeared to have led a drunken life. He was a tanner in the employ of Messrs. Tinsley, and 18 months ago in consequence of his drunkenness his wife had to leave him. He afterwards went to her, and asked her to take him back. Even then be was drunk, but for the sake of the children she took him back again. Since then he had been on the spree from time to time, and in Jelly last, prior to taking out the summons he lost his employment inconsequence of his drunkenness. Having been drunk the prisoner was fined ss. and costs. A. separation order was also granted, Hewitt to pay Ss. a week towards the maintenance of the wife, who will have the custody of the children.

div.head: SEPARATION.AT WARRINGTON, ,
div.p: SEPARATION.AT WARRINGTON, ,

—.— At the Warrington Police Court on Wednesday, Ann Boardman, Liverpool-road, was granted a separation order from her husband on the ground that he was art. habitual drunkard.—Mr. Steel, on behalf of the com- plainant, said that owing to the defendant's drunken habits he had lost a good situation. Since January he had not done any work"and had spent nearly £lOO. He was continually drinking, and it seemed to be a hope- less case, as everything had been done to try and reform him, but without avail.

div.head: STERN_ PARENT.
div.p: THE STERN_ PARENT.

The love-miking of a Widnes porter named Harry Forder, employed at the Fidler's Ferry Station, near Warrington. had its sequel at the Warrington County Petty Sessions onWednesday,whon Frederick Daniels of Penketh, was summoned for assault. Forder stated that on the night of the 6th inst. the defendant's daughter came to the station to meet a friend, who failed to pat in an appearance. The night being dark, she asked him to take her a part of the way home, as she was frightened. On the way home they mat her father, who without any warning, assaulted him, striking him in the face and on the head with his fist.—Defendant said he objected to the complainant making love to his daughter, who was only fifteen years of age. When he met them he simply boxed his daughter's ears and pushed the complainant away.—The magistrates dis- missed the case.

div.head: 4. it" TOO 'WEAK TO SrAND."
div.p: 4. it" TOO 'WEAK TO SrAND."
Debilitatel Mother's Remarkable Sto:y of Saffering, ani Her Cure by Bile Beans.

Mrs. Hambleton, of Bishopsworth-road,Bristol,says "A year or so back my health was very much affected through family troubles. I was attended by a doctor for two months, but 1 got no better. I sank to such extreme weakness that I couldn't even walk across a room, and the least exeltion made me faint right away. If I managed to eat a little food I was dreadfully sib!: afterwards. I suffered terribly from headaches, and I became very thin and pale. Directly I lay down in bed at night the most terrible spasms seized me. First a felling of great heat ran through me from heat to foot, followed by an awful feeling of cold, and I shivered all over. "During the daytime. I was completely worn out. I was too weak to look after my children. Then I was persuaded to try Bile Beans. I hadn't taken many Beans before I feld a decided improvement, so I continued Bile Beans until I was as strong and well as possible.'

div.head: WARRINGTON BURIAL SOCIETY.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON BURIAL SOCIETY.

' I The members of the above Society assembled at the British Workman Public-house, Iforsernarket-street on Monday, the occasion being the 35th anniversary, of the establishment of the Society. The attendance was exceedingly good. the meeting being presided over by the President, Mr. Joseph Mather, who was supported by the Vice-President, Mr. Thomas Basker- ville, jun., Treasurer, Mr. James Parr ; trustees, Messrs. Peter Edgar, William Eakersley, Mr. James Gresty ; tuditor,Hr. Joseph Adams; general secretary, Mr. Lawrence Weir and others. The Chairman in his opening address congratulated the members upon the working of the Society for the past-year. Sc . expressed the pleasure it gave him since he had been elected to that honourable position to be associated with the other officials who had alwayis sho-vn a desire to work amicably with those' arouad them and to do all that lay in their power to further the interests of the Society. Tue substantial gain which the S iciety bud made during the year was such that every mern'oer he felt sure would feel proud, and the general outlook of the Society was full of hope and encouragement. In conclusion he hoped the Soeiety would continue to prosper and felt assured with the officets and secretary they had at the head they would be able at the end of • next year to even show better results. (Applause.) The General Secretary, Mr. Lawrence Weir, presented his annual report which showed that the Society's funds now amounted to £3,26D 121. 7,1. compared with £3,053 19s. 20. for the year previous a gaiii 0f,..£2/13 13s. sd. The numerical c mdition wis 1,435 com- pared with 1,421 last year. The report further showed that the Seciety had paid away in death claims £77 10s. compared with $63 ss. the previous year, and that they had invested in the Corporation and ! upon mortgage £2,850. The Secretary in conclusion • briefly pointed out the advantages gained under their • nawly constructed table of benefits and how effectively it was touching the class it was intended to reach. Several claims had been paid for 25 years membership during the year. He earnestly apt, 'aled to the members to leave no stone unturned in preasing forward their claims upon the public under such tables. The auditors reported that the accounts and register kept by the General Secretary, and also the books of the Treasurer and collectors had been examined and had pleasure in testifying that the same were correct and satisfactory. The bank books, , ! Corporation bonds, mortgage investments, and vouchers had been presente I for inspection, and the same wers in perfect order.—ln the election of officers Mr. Thomas Biskerville was unanimously elected president and Mr. Joseph Ashton vice-president for the year, Mr. Joseph Adams being again elected auditor. A very lengthy and interesting agenda was g ‘ne through, comprising several notices of motion on which a very lively discussion took place, and the following members took part : Messrs. Peter Edgar, William Eckersley, Joseph Ashton, Thomas Miller, William Hall, John Jones, Joseph Adams, Frederick Massey, and others. A. vote of thanks was accorded to the retiring president, Mr. Joseph Mather for the courteous msnner in which he had conducted the busi mess during his term of office.

div.head: SEASIDE DANGER.
div.p: A SEASIDE DANGER.
Salt Water Causes Skin Disease— Severe Case Cured by Zam-Buk.

The action of salt water upon some skins is ' dangerously injurious, coda peculiar form of eczema or tissue-poisoning frequently arises. Mr. R. Owen, of 14, Sondes- street, Portland-street, Westmorland-road, Walwor th, London, S.W., said to a City pressman "When I was seven years of age, my parents took me to Sheerness, and immediately after my return to London an eruption broke out on my legs. Sores formed and though we tried first one thing and then another, no permanent good resulted. Ultimately I commenced to visit a well-known hospital. I derived no benefit from the treatment, and afterwards attended three other hospitals with the same result. It was said that I was suffering from salt-water poisoning. At sixteen my legs got worse. Tee inflammation extended from ankles to knees, and the irritation was unbearable. I went to a skin hospital, but still got no relief, and I felt my health giving way altogether. "In November lest I was given a small quantity of Zam-Buk. I applied the balm two or three times, and to my delight the itching and inflammation began to di* away. The wounds looked like healing, so I perse- vered with Zsm-Buk, and in four or five weeks my legs were completely cured." div.head: GtNERAL BOOTH AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: GtNERAL BOOTH AT WARRINGTON.
CIVIC WELCOME AND PUBLIC MEETING.
The Secret of "The Army's" Success.

Warrington did honour on Tuesday to the veteran founder and head of the Salvation ArMy—General Booth. Although he has attained ,his seventy-eighth year the General is stile hale and hearty and he is at present engaged in a motor campaign from Inverness to Plymouth. Everywhere he has met with remark- , ably enthusiastic receptions, testifying to the respect and affection with which he is universally regarded. On Tuesday he motored from Rochdale to Warrington by a seventy miles route, addressing meetings at! several places where great crowds awaited him. I During the afternoon the weather was anything but ; favourable and at Bowden a severe thunderstorm was experienced. It was close upon half-pst seven when the General and his staff entered Warrington via Knutsford-road and the welcome extended I was cordial in the extreme. The main streets were thronged add when the cars came into view hearty cheers wire raised. The General, ! *ith his flowing white beard, is a striking figure and he was soon recognized when he appeared, in the famous " white car." He stood up and waved his hands in acknowledgment of the acclaims of the multitide. At the Town Hall there was a civic recep- tion. Before the General's arrival the Salvation Army band played selections on the lawn and there was a good muster of army workers. Many well-known 1 townspeople had assembled at the top of the Town Hall steps and when the General was seen approach- ing, the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Bolton) came out to receive him, accompanied by the mace and sword bearers. Tn9,,head of the Army did not look at all exhausted after his long journey and, along with several members of his staff, quickly acceuded the steps. Among the officers present were: Commissioners Nicols and Cadman, , Brigadier Cox, Colonels Lawley and Edie, and Adjutant and Mrs. Cooper (Warrington). The General shook hands with the Mayor and Hayoress--•ind his worship expressed the pleasure which it afforded all to see him once more in Warrington. The Mayoress handed the General a box of beautiful orchids which he accepted with thanks, afterwards shaking hands with many other 1 ladies and gentlemen who stood around him. General Boom then delivered a short speech in which he said his aim was to rouse in the minds of the people who had time, leisure and means a desire to pro- mote the welfare of the masses of the people. In his journey from Inverness he had seen indications of want of thrift,cleanlinoss, &c., which had much to do with the welfare, health, and happiness of the community. They could all do something to rnal...e "Lnerrie England" merrier still, and better, and her people more powerful for good. It was his object and aim to do something to stir up the minds of the people to those practical questions which hart- a very great deal to do with the happiness and with the religion of the people. He aimed at doing some good. He was grateful to God for, enabling him to do what he had done, and he could say in His presence, that the joy of his life was to do good to his fellow creatures. In conclusiet the General said: "God bless you all ;amen." He then bade good-bye to the Mayor and Mayoress and left for the meeting at the Parr Hall. '

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, August 18, 1906. WOMAN'S REALM.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, August 18, 1906. WOMAN'S REALM.

that another General had stepped into his shoes. (Cheers.) They would not talk of dying, bat of living. The General illustrated the success which the Army had achieved by giving a large number of interesting instanoes. In the first place they dealt with those out- side the pale of ordinary religious effort, with the churchless crowds. Oh ! it was a melancholy fact that in every part of the world the trend of the masses of the people, of the hard-handed, horny-handed sons of toil was to keep away ;rom the churches and missions. Were they to leave them to fall over the precipice of damnation without a warning? God forbid. The Salvation was so orgy-sized that they could follow people to their haunts of pleasure, and their homes and try to compel them, whether they would or would not, to come in and hear about their condition and to accept the mercy and the salvation that had teal provided for I them. The Army was a force which permeated the masses, humanized them, and saved them from despair and self-destruction. (Applause!. Daring the last few years £1,250,000 had been spent in England to build inebriates homes, and to carry out a scheme which had been a miserable failure. If that • money had been handed over to the Salvation Army they would have something to show for it. They had done a great deal in the direction of the reclamation lof drunkards, but it was all very well to commit the refuse of the country to the care of the Army, and leave an old General to beg for the money to pay the bill. Dealing especially with the question of putting the people on the land, he said that some people contended that that could not be done, but General Booth had succeeded in doing many things, and his dreams had a / knack of coming wonderfully true, and one gentleman ! had trusted him with £lOO,OOO with which to make the I experiment. (Laughter and applause). If there was no I land to be found in sufficient quantities here, across the seas there were millions and millions of acres that were crying out for men and women to till them and for children to laugh and dance upon them. And in that direction their thoughts turned to the Colonies. Last year 13,00) people were sent to Canada. (Applause.) lt was urged ItEsinst them that Ithey were taking away the best blood of the country, perhaps that was so, but 'what was the good of having the best blood in the country if they had to keep them out of the rates. (Applause). Dealing again with the secret of the success of the Army, the General alluded to its marvellous organiza- tion, and said the bold, open and avowed movement that they wished to rescue attracted the notice and confidence of the people. They did not poach upon other peoples dominions. They went down into the horrible pit and brought up the material which did not belong to any- one. Another secret of success was the self-sacrificing efforts of his officers—officers with hearts and brains, and with confidence in God to raise and save the fallen. Another was their Incromitable and Untiring Spirit, no fewer than 8,000 public-houses being visited in this country aione every Saturday night. (Applause.) They had had to fight and were fighting. Their methods had helped them and yet they bad had heaped upon them abloquy and contempt and yet they were reaching and benefiting the submerged crowds. In conclusion, the speaker asked the audience what they had done for the Army, and appealed for support from all classes of the community. It was all right to help their own church and ministers, but surely something was left for the General and his Army. (Cheers.) VOTES OE THANKS.

Alderman FORSHAW, in moving a vote of thanks to the "Grand Old Man of The Salvation Arms" for his most interesting and able lecture, said the tieneral was the founder of a most excellent,noble and Christian work. It was founded entirely upon selfishness, and dealt with the waifs and strays, the halt and the blind. They all hoped, and sincerely hoped, General Booth would be spared for many years to continue his good and noble work. (Cheers.)
Councillor Z.-VANS seconded, and the motion was unanimously and heartily agreed to, the audience rising en mane.

The GENERAL briefly retuned thinks, and proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. ThOrnton for presiding over the meeting, and this motion was carried with equal enthusiasm. A collection having been taken on behalf of the funds of the Army the Doxology was sung, and the meeting terminated.
The General thea left for Penketh, being the guest of Mrs. Robert Garnett.
On Monday morning a large crowd witnesSed the General's departure for Crewe via Chester, he being heartily cheered as his car passed through the Park gates.

div.p: WINWICK ASYLUM. £21,000 Wanted for an Extension.
DRESS-FASHION-HOME,
A GREAT DANISH PIANIST.

Madame Johanna Stockmarr, the famous Danish pianist, is a friend and favourite of Queen Alexandra, with whom she always plays the piano a great deal. She was born in Copenhagen, where her father was a well-known, violinist. She herself tried to play the piano almost before she could speak, and she was sent to the Copenhagen Conservatoire when about fourteen, where she studied under Professor Helsteid. Later on she went to Paris, and since her return to Denmark has played in Paris, Germany, and all over Scan- dinavia. She gave her first recital here two years ago, at which the Queen and some other members of the Royal Family were present, and received quite an ovation lately at the Grieg Orchestral Concert. THE UP-TO-DATE ,MAEIC.

The sleeve is quite the distinguishing feature of smart up-to-date attire, and its shape and style go far to mark the difference between the modish or dowdy appearance of its wearer. The sleeves pictured in our illustration are selected from among the newest and smartest models, many of them forming -part of the latest auturfan costumes. At the top comes a sleeve which is well calculated to form part of the necessary renovation of a last year's autumn frock. The sleeve proper is made of some pretty contrasting material, such as crêpe or velvet, and the cros- sing bands of the fabric of which the gown is made. Next comes the latest thing in long coat sleeves. The two next models are intended to form part of an indoor costume, and both ter- minate a little below the elbow. At the right

hand is a lace affair suitable for a dressy toilet or a dinner-gown. The long sleeve in the middle has its fulness taken into a .succession of tucks below the elbow. It is intended for a plain morning gown. The remaining sleeves are smart. examples Of the up-to-date sleeve for afternoon attire. Both would lend themselves admirably to renovations.

div.head: " NEW " WOMAN.
div.p: THE " NEW " WOMAN.

Bishop Welldon, the new Dean of Manchester, has expressed himself most wisely about the kind of woman who is generally described as "new." He says he sees rio reason why a woman who smokes, apes masculine clothing, boards plat- forms, and goes hatless about the streets and into churches should be regarded as a shocking person. He should rather say that she is to be pitied, because in his opinion she displayed ex- traordinary poverty of mind and lacked qualities that her most commonplace sisters possessed, says the Lady's Pictorial. For women, as he pointed out, were given physical attractions far greater than men; their strength lies in their womanlinesa and the difference their order of mind. When, therefore, a woman simply imitated the other sex she gave up her independence of mind and lost the honour that was hers Iny, right. This is a really sensible view of a weart- somely discussed question. PEACOCES' FEATHERS. Peacocks' feathers are quite "the thing" in the feminine world of London to-day, although Paris discarded them for ostrich plumes quite a month ago. We are always behind the French capital in these matters. There has been such a rush for these ornaments lately that it is puzzling to know where they all come from, and it is inte- resting to learn that Paris supplies beautiful arti- ficial plumes which the vainest peacock would be proud to wear. These cost from Bs. to 12s. a bundle. Real ones only cost a guinea, and a bundle of the very cheapest might be obtained for ss. 11d. Meanwhile, the fair Parisienne is captivating promenaders in the Bois with her ostrich feathers, which instead of being curled round the hat, as was formerly the case, are fastened in front or at the side, and sweep grace- fully behind right down to the waist. A. CREPE-DE-CHINE BLOUSE.

A very smart, dainty, and becoming after- noon •blouse for the early atitumn i the subject of our illustration. The material of which it is made is a thick, firm, washing crepe-de-chine, of a charming ivory tone. Round the shoulders is arranged a deep shaped yoke of the crepe-de- chine, finishing in front in a long •tabbed point. This yoke, as well as the folded neckband, is adorned with bands of heavy ivory guipure, bor- dered on either edge with large French knots

• worked in thick ivory silk. The bottom of the yoke and the long ; tab are also adorned with French knots. The blouse proper is gathered on to this yoke, and allowed to fall in soft folds to the waist. The sleeves, .of elbow-length, con- sist of full puffs of the crepe-de-chine crossed by bands 'of insertion, 'lliad are set into cuffs of the same guipure finished with little lace frills. A final touch is given to the blouse by the intro- duction, just beneath the tabbed end, of a large bow of ribbon, matching in colour the particular skirt with which the blouse is worn.

since I offered to send to any of my Members a free bottle of Mason's Extract of Herbs. Well, I have received a large number of applications and have now only a few left. If any of you wish to receive a bottle, write me at once, and it shall be sent post free. During this hot weather you will find that this non-alcoholic drink is delicious. Tom and Harry had been, spending the ft fortnight of their summer holiday with th grandfather. Their home was in London, so was always a treat to pay a vieit to the lit
Ale ouse in the country village, where g,randfs.thcr ived, with only his servant, Anne, to look after him.

The boys were in the orchard one morniaig looking at the early apples. "I do feel hot and thirsty !" Harry said. "Let us see if there are any apples down."' Now, there was only one tree on which the fruit was. ripe. Grandfather called it the "early August" tree. It was covered with most delicious juicy apples, but the boys were only allowed to have those which had fallen. As they had paid many visits to the tree that morning, there did not seem nadich chance of finding any more on the ground. "Not a single one!" said Torn, with a sigh. "I- wish a good old wind would spring up." "Just look at the ripe apples on that branoh," said Harry, pointing to where they were bang- • ing in a tempting fashion. "I do think it a shame.we are never allowed to pick one," Tom grumbled, "and we have only a day or two left before we go home." , "No chance of apples then!!' his brother said; "It will be a lon-, time before we see any there; aid when we do, it ia not the same as , having them fresh 'off the tree. I vote we shake a few, down."
t, and
Yours sincerely,' "Lucy FITZPAIMICS-
ABQU BEN ADHEM. Abou Bert Adhem; may his tribe icrease,.

, Awoke one night from a deep dream of peace, And saw within the moonlight in his room, Alaking_it rich, like a lily in bloom, An angel, writing in a book of gold. Exceeding peace had made Ben. Adhem bold, And so to the presence in the room he said, NY-hat writest thou? The vision raised its
head, And with a look, full of all sweet accord, Answered, "The names of those who love the
Lord." • "And is mine one ? " cried Abou. "Nay, not

so, Replied the angel. Abou spoke more low, But cheerily still, said,. "I pray thee then, Write me as one that loves his fellow men." The angel wrote, and vanished.' The next night It came again, with a great awakening light, And showed the names whom love of God had
blest, And lo! Ben Adhem's name led all the rest.

Dear Uncle.—l am writing this letter to thank you for the box of chocolates sent me. They arrived this morning, and served as a surprise to me. Last night I arrived home from my, holidays at Scarboro', I stayed a week, and I saw the Channel Fleet. I close my letter, with thanke from YoUr loving niece, LIZZIE WILLS,

, A CERTAIN LITTLE GIRL, There. is a very little girl, With cheeks of rose and white, Whose sunny hair shows many a curl, Whose eyes are blue and bright; A pretty girl, a bonnie girl, But oh I a naughty sprite!

" All right; here goes!" and Ton seized a branch and gave it a gentle shake. Nothing, fell, however, and then the two boys' took hold of the bqugh and shook it as hard as they could. Dawn the apples came this time, and they began to fill their pockets. "I was wondering what made such aosudden gale of wind spring up," said a voice, and there stood grandfather, who had just • acme through the gate inte the orchard. Tom and Harry hung their heads, and looked very guilty. "So this is the way you youngsters obey my orders," the old gentleman went on. ." We never did it before, really, grandfather," Tom said, "but we were very thirsty, and the apples .did look So jolly." Harry had a large piece in his mouth, speech was impossible. "I thought I could trust you boys," grand-f father said, "now come up into the loft, 1 have something to show you." They climbed the outside steps after him, and there, in the aira light, they g&Nir two large hampers, "I did not forbid you to pick the fruit because I, wanted to deny you any pleasure," grandfather said, "but I hoped to fill these hampers for you to take home." "We are sorry," Tom said, and both he and Harry looked much ashamed of themselves. They felt how wrong it was to have disobeyed grandfather, especially as all the time he had been planning such kind things for them. "Very well, we will not say any more about the matter," the old gentleman said. "No doubt the temptation was strong, and you thought it a little hard the fruit was forbidden. Only, boys, will you try to remember we older folks generally have some reason for what we forbid, and it is for your pleaeure and good, ansi not for our own, that mks are made '4 " I remain, your loving niece, LIZZIE MASON.. Dear Mr. Eclitor,—l am sending you a 1.,0ce of poetry, which I hope you will like. It is call"' " Abou Ben Adhem."

div.head: STAR, STODGE, AND STIVER.
div.p: STAR, STODGE, AND STIVER.

I Star, Stodge, and Stiver were three puppies, who were so lively and troublesome that from the day of their birth they made their sedate old mother's life a burden to her. It is true they were a fine trio, that any one might be pioud c,and yet before six weeks were-Tonb by, Mrs. Bess (their mother) was nearly worn to a shadow. The farm on which they all lived was not a large one; in fact, it was mainly devoted to the rearing of fowls, and these were the cause of all the trouble.' Chickens of all sorts of breeds and sizes were to be seen every- where and these three naughty pups had a rmly-rooted idea that the only reason why chickens were allowed on the face of the earth was to give young puppies a little chance of fun. At length trouble came to the farmer's 0 ears. Three chickens, each fine ones ot their kind, had been killed by the ruthless dogs, and their master, Mr. Sancroft, hit on an ex- pedient for curing them of the habit. It was this: A strong piece of string was tied to each of their necks, at the other end of which a dead chicken was tied, and this they were unable to get rid of for three days. In vain did they pull and bite those strings. It was Aar too strong to break, and their small teeth were much too soft to bite them; and so the chickens remained where they were. The puppies tried to get help and sympathy. from 1 Mrs. Bess, but she refused to gnaw the sirings, and plainly told them that they richly deserved the punishment that they had received for not doing as they ought; so they ran away to the big barn and hid themselves away in the hay. It was here that a grand idea came to Stodge. As he lay in the sweet-smelling hay, he watched the timid little mice running about, and then the large rats ventured also. Stodge remembered then that his mother had often said, "My children, if ever you wish to chase anything, mind you chase rats and mice; this will please our master better than I anything else." Mice and rats were poor fun to chickens, the puppies had thought, and had taken no notice of them, until now. The next day the puppies hunted the barn; the dead 1 chickens .had been taken away, and they were free at last; and though they lost the first mouse through an accident to Stiver, yet before long the barn was practically free of rats and mice as long as the puppies lived on the farm.
From your loving nephew,
ARTHUR FEARN.

div.head: HOLIDAY SONG.
div.p: A HOLIDAY SONG.

The time is coming; sing, boys, "Hurrah!" When away from school we'll hie, " Hurrah Away we'll rush with laugh and song, , For the days are happy, the time is long. That free from care we'll merril3 play; Nor think of books the live-long day. Then merrily shout' Hurrah " boys, Right merrily shout "Hurrah "

From morn till eve, when the skies are clear, We'll ramble and frolic without a fear; We'll chase the rabbit along the hedge, And track wildfowl in the reedy sedge; We'll snare the fish in the silver brook, And away to the wind with slate and book. Oh! merrily shout " Hurrah I " boys, Bight Merrily shout " Hurrah ! " When evening comes with redd'ning gleam, We'll take us off to the clear, cold stream; And into its depths we'll dive and swim, Till, ruddy of face and supple of limb, The deepening twilight shall call us home, Till another sun rouse us again to roam. Then merrily shout " Hurrah I" boys, Right merrily shout " Hurrah 1"

placed in a stable. It Invariably happen l that spokes and pedals become Viterlaced, that Grit). meters are broken off, and gear-cases grievously dented in, while any endeavour to extricate a mount at the back of the stack involves exaspera• tion and delay. Astonishing Cycle Accidents.

Although the number of cycling accidents is infinitesimally small in proportiou to the number of those who ride daily, not a few of those reported seem to arise from the utter folly of the riders concerned. It is related that a Ruabon lady, riding a free wheel for the first time, neglected to use her brakes, and was run away with down a steep hill and killed. From Ireland comes the story of a young lady liar> from Enniscrone to Ballina. Haring ts cross ,to the wrong side of the road to avoid a cart, the young lady continued to descend a hill on her wrong side, despite the fact that she saw a man on bieycle slowly ascending on his proper side. Iler shrieks being unheeded by the approaching cyclist, and the lady holding on her course, a tremendous collision occurred„fortunately unattended by fatal results, although both machines were,wrecked.

div.head: Lady Cyclist mid the Temp.
div.p: The Lady Cyclist mid the Temp.

"Maid o' the Moor" offers her lady readers some reassuring advice concerning the tramp and his habits. It is true that many lady cyclists, when alone, entertain a great dread of tramps, whose appearance alone is often sufficient to cause dis- quietude. Accoraincr to "Maid o' the Moor's" experience, however, the tramp has a preference for main high roads rather than sequestered by- ways, and is much too jealous of maintaining his liberty during the summer months to be likely to interfere with a girl on a bicycle. At the same time, the advice is given to ride quietly and steadily on when seeing a tramp on the road, with- out showing any sign of fear. "We have all met the yapping dog, who yaps all the more at those who run away from him. The tramp is the same kind of, animal—and the girl who loOks as if she expected him to molest her runs the most risk of being molested."

the committee is acting wisely in trying to perpetuate old landmarks. Continuing the Alderman thought it was a pity when they changed the name of Slutchers% lane into Arpley-street, as the former was the old, original form in which the name appeared in a map of Warrington over GOO years old. With regard to Palmyra- square, the change was made to avoid a multiplicity of names.
• The minutes were confirmed. LAMP-LIGHTERS' WAGES.

Councillor WRIGHT asked the Chairman of the Gas Committee :—Are the lamplighters being paid the minimum wages of 21s. in accordance with special resolution passed December sth, 1905,exclusive of Sun- day work ? Councillor DUNCAN, moving the adoption of the minutes; said the lamp-lighters were paid the usual full wages.
RECORD GAS PROFITS. A PLEA FOR THE CONSUMER.

The Gas Committee's minutes included the annual report o: the Gas Engineer (Mr. W. S. Haddock) which showed a record profit of over £14,000. Councillor Clam G said he was pleased to see the Gas Committee making such progress and collecting such a great amount of money towards the rates. He thought the time bad arrived when certain amounts might be fixed to go towards Ors reduction of the rates, and after that let the consumers have some benefit. (Hear, hoar.) He noticed the Gas Engineer suggested there should be setae replating done at Longford, but he thought the consumers ought to have prior claim. He (Councillor Clegg) had been comparing the cost per cubic foot of gas. According to the returns of Mr. Haddock, the cost was somewhat less than for some time past. No more money was being paid for the manufacture of gas. That meant that all the employees had had to be satis- fied with the amount of money they had previously got, but he noticed the salaries seemed to have crept up wonderfully during the last few years. He had looked into the figures for the year 1904-5 as to the cost of gas per 1,000 feet and found they did not agree witb the figures submitted to the Council. Pehaps some explana- tion could be given. The MAYOR pointed out that the salaries were less than last vest. After looking at the figures mentioned by Councillor Clegg he said there 'was a discrepancy. Alderman BRYNETT said the reduction of the price of gas was a consummation devoutly to be wished but he thought in face of the Engineer's recommendation the time was not opportune. Owing to the discrepancy mentioned by Councillor Clegg, it was agreed that the report should be sent back.

div.head: TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: TOWN COUNCIL.
A SHORT MEETING.
Preserving an Old Street Name.

The Warrington Town Council was in holiday mood on Friday evening and half an hour sufficed for the transaction ef the business of the monthly meeting.' The Mayor (Alderman Bolton) presided and there were also present :—The Mayor, Aldermen A. Bennett, John Evans, H. W. Fmncomb, W. Pierpoint ; Councillors J. Ball. W. Benson, T. Burton, T. Chantler, W. Clegg, E. Cunningtou, D. S. Duncan, James Evans, L. Ellisou,,T. J. Hulse, Dr. Joseph, J. Lord, J. Maginn, J. Pemberton, J. Sankey, Skelland, J. F. Smith, 1. Stott, J. T. \Vilding, J. Wilkinson, W. J. Wilson ; Messrs. A. T. Hallaway (deputy town clerk), J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), T. Longdin (borough surveyor), and W, S. Haddock (gas engineer). A CLEAR FIELD FOR GENERAL BOOTH.

The Miron said that one reason for calling the Council meeting for that night was because General Booth would be in Warrington on Tuesday evening, and he did not think that they could have both General Boot Wand the Council meeting on the same night. (Laughter):

div.head: LEASE OF LAND.
div.p: LEASE OF LAND.

The Finance and Estate Committee reported that an application having been made by the Warrington Motor Carriage Company, Limited, for a lease of the land behind the Education Offices, the site of stables recently nemolished,it was resolved to offer the company the whole of the land between the Education, Offices and the boundary well for a five years tenancy at £26 per annum, and charge them 55. per annum acknowledgment for the right of way up Gsrven-place. The company had written accepting these terms. Alderman BENNETT moved the adoption of the minutes, and Councillor WILKINSON seconded. Councillor EVANS said that having regard to the position of the land be did not think it was wise that the Finance Committee should enter into a lease for Ave years. He moved that the minutes referring to the lease be referred back to the committee. The amendment was seconded by Alderman PIRRPOINT. Alderman BENsarr Said that tne Vinance Committee thought that this piece of land would not be required within the term of the lease for any public purposes. It was only a little bit of land, and the committee thought that they were simply doing the best they could with the Corporation property, for the 01110 being. "Councillor EVANS said he did not think it was wise for the Finance Connnittee to tie the hands of the Corporation. The MATOR : You think the annual tenancy would be better than a five year's letise ? Councillor Evans : Yes, we should not tie our pro- perty in Sankey-street. e Councillor LORD Midi he understood that the sug- gested lessees wanted to build a kind of temporary shed and were most anxious to get on with it at ORM Unless Councillor Evans could give some urgent reasons why it should not be let, or could show that the Street Improvement Committee had a scheme to use this land they ought to let it be leased. The MA.vOrt put the amendment, which was lost, only two members voting in favour. The minutes were then put and adopted. COLONEL EDELSTEN'S WRIT.

The Street Improvement and Lighting Committee on July sth discussed at considerable length theagreeinent with Colonel Edelsten, and it was ultimately decided that the opinion of counsel should be taken as to the position of the Corporation, the case to be first .suh- mitted to the committee. The case for the opinion of counsel respecting the action commenced by Mr. J. A. Ede!sten against the Corporation and Mr. William Bolton was submitted to the committee on 19th July and it was resolved," That the Mayor be empowered to obtain independent professional advice and assistance with,regatd to his position in the action." At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee the Town Clerk reported that he had been served with a writ at the suit of 111 r. J. A. Edelsten, in which the. Mayor was joined as a defendent, claiming specific per- formance of the agreement of the 3rd October, 1904,nnd the damages, Sm. The minutes were approved without oomment. " LOUCHER'S LANE." AN qLD NAME.

The Street I mprovernest Committee resolved that \the new road leading from Wilderspool to the Bridge over the Runcorn and Latchford Canal he called Loucher's-lane. Resolved that Chapel-street on the north side of Queen's Gardens be renamed Palmyra- square. Alderman BENNETT said the first recommendation was an adherence—and he thought a very proper one— to the old name of the lane. Ilia impression was it was jnht as well to retain the original name. Alderman PIEUPOINT : It is not " Loucher "at all. Alderman ENS ETT : I don't know whether this is the correct way to spell it, but lam told it is I think

div.head: FIRE AT WHITECROSS.
div.p: THE FIRE AT WHITECROSS.
The Fire Brigade Committee had had before them a report by Superintendent Turner on the fire at White- cross, and had decided that the Warrington Brigade was not to blame in the matter. _ . _

_ In moving the adoption of the minutes, Councillor BURTON said he believed what the Superintendent stated was quite correct, but, there seemed to be a certain amount of muddling and mistakes somewhere. The minutes were approved. NEW ELECTRICAL PLANT.

In moving the adoption of the Electricity and Tram- ways Committee, Alderman SIVIETkitYRST referred to the new high tension plant which has lust been installed. It consisted, he said, of one steam turbo by the British Westinghouse Co., of 400 h.p. coupled direct to 3 phase alternating current generater of 300 kwts, running at a speed of 3,000 revolutions per minute ; one motor alternator of 100 lc wts. capacity, by the Brush Electrical Engineering Co.' and one extra high tension switch- board, supplied by the British Thomson Houston Co. Thiamin of the latest and most up-to-date design, being absolutely safe and perfectly fire-proof. Three and a Quarter miles of extra high tension cable supplied by the St. Helens Cable and Rubber Co.' Ltd., had been laid,and extended as far as the Warrington Lay-by. This included a piece of special submarine cable laid across the lay-bye' from a point at the end of Greenalrs, avenue, to the river bank opposite. All of the work had been carried out to Mr. Mathias's specification and under his personal supervision. Councillor Wilkinson seconded and the minutes were adopted. THE TRAMWAYS.

The Board of Trade wrote agreeing to a further extension of time (twelve months) for the completion of the tramways. Alderman BENNETT : Does this refer to the Man- chester-road and Padgate-lane route? Alderman SMETHURST : No, to the Stockton Heath extension.
LIGHT WANTED IN POACHER'S-LANE. MORE LAMPS WANTED.

Coon cillor ELLisoN moved that the Street Improve meat And Lighting Committee be 'requested to under- take the arrangement of gas lamps in Lower Wash and Westy lanes, also an additional lamp in Poachers-lane, in thcaatchford Ward. He said that it was over two years since his attention was drawn by a deputation from the residents in that locality to the fact that a re-arrangement of gas lamps was required, and he at once communicated the information to the Chairman of the Lighting Committee. At different times since then he had, both by letter and word, drawn attention to the questiom, and he had been reminded so many times by different persons regarding the delay, which had occurred that he decided to place the matter on the agenda in order to give the chairman an opportunity to explain the cause of the delay and also vindicate his own position in the matter. The 31.i.v0n thought the Comrnitte might take this matter into consideration as a recommendation. Alderman PIERPOINT said Councillor Ellison's motion was an indictment of the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee. He had been a member of the Committee and had been struck by the capable way in which it performed its duty. The lilAvort : The resolution is not seconded yet. Alderman PIERPOINT : I will second it. (Laughter). Councillor EVANS said one lamp had already been placed in the Lower Wash. The residents had probably seen the improvements which had been made in street lighting elsewhere and wanted some of those improve- ments for themselves. As soon as possible the Com- mittee would attend to the matter. Aldermon PIERPOINT : Where is the Lower Wash ? (Laughter). Alderman BEWNF:TT mild it must be very necessary to provide an additional lamp in Poacher's-lane. (Laughter). Councillor ELLTION said that he simply wished to achieve his object and would withdraw his resolution in view for the assurance received from Councillor Evans.

div.head: WATERED WHISKY.
div.p: WATERED WHISKY.
Unsuccessful Prosecution at Stockton Heath.

At the Direshury Petty Sessions, at Stockton Heath, on Tuesday, Joseph Broady, licensee of the Cat and Lion, Stretton, was summoned for selling whisky which was adulterated by the addition of ten per cent. of water.—Defendant was represented by Mr. Browne. Ernest Jeffs, assistaat inspector of weights and measures, spoke to visiting the defendant's premises and purchasing a pint of Scotch whisky. This was divided into three parts, ove of which was analysed. By Mr. Browne : He did not see a notice in the bar which said that the spirits sold were of a superior quality hut were not guaranteed as to strength, being adulterated with water acc,,rding to price. Mr. Browne said that some eighteen months ago an extra duty WtlS put upon spirits with the result that whilst distillers of special whiskies did not advance their prices they reduced the strength. Defendant was in the habit of buying his whisky in bottles, there not being a sufficient demand to warrant its being pur- chased in larger quantities. The whisky he diluted by the addition of 22 percent. of water which before the distillers reduced the strength was a fit quantity to add. Not knowing that the strength had been reduced it was a pure mistake on the defendants part that he added too much water. Defendant bad a large notice in the bar to the effect that the sprits were not guaranteed, as they were diluted and a similar notice also hung in his bar parlour.— Defendant and his brother-in-law who assisted him in his business both spoke as to. the presence of the notice in the bar, and the magistrates, being satisfied that the notice was hung in a conspicu- I ous place dismissed the summons.

div.head: Reform or Disestablishment.
div.p: Reform or Disestablishment.

Sir,—l have read with much interest your commenta about the "Evangelical Fear," that if an attempt isl made to enforce the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Church Discipline it may lead to Dis-, establishment. Well, assuming that it will, do the Evangelicals think that Disestablishment can be worse for the Church than the domination of Romanising clergy and unrestrained lawlessness? As a Churchman. I am confident that thousands of the laity would prefer disestablishment to a continuance of the present state of things. Are these Ritualists so blind and so forgetful of the lessons of history as to imagine that the Established Church or any other Church will ever again be allowed to defy the law? In 1534 an Act was passed called "Act for the submission of the clergy," and here we are nearly five centuries later actually dis- cussing the same thing. What a position for a nation which boasts so much about progress, enlightenment, and wise government. What shall we say of a body of men who instead of teaching and preaching obedience and respect for the law are themselves the law breakers? When I read for the first time Buckle's" History of Civilisation," I wondered whether he was a little too severe on the clergy, where he shows with such a mass of historical evidence, and with such a consumate presentation of facts that in every age, in every country, the clergy and more especially the ecclesiastical courts and councils, have clogged the wheels of progress, have fought step by step everything which was calculated to accelerate the march of intellect. I begin to realise that Buckle was right, and that disestablishment is the only practical and logical remedy. But let us take another line of argument. Are not Church of England clergymen very shortsighted in trying to kick away the foundation upon which they stand? How illogical and irrational are these attempts to get above the law which has provided them with livings, and, which has so long protected hundreds of worthless and incompetent men. How absurd is the contention of some clerical writers that the English Church was not established by law. "The Church of England," said Freeman " is above and beyond all other Churches of Europe, the child of the Church of Rome." Then came the quarrel between Henry VIII. and the Pope,followed by an "Act for the restraint of appeals to Rome." Then came the Act I have referred to in which the clergy " promised (in verbo sacerdotii) that they will never from henceforth presume to attempt, enact, put in use, promulgate or execute any new canon or constitution unless the King's consent and license bad been gtanted for their so doing." This being so, is it not wilful misrepresenta- tion of facts to pretend that the church is not subject to the law of the laud? In conclosion let me earnestly appeal to all who value liberty of conscience and hate dogmatism to resist in every possible way this baneful Romeward tendency. Of one thing we may be absolutely certain, that salvation can never be assured by adopt- ing any exclusive form of religion, and of all forms, that which consists of an endless round of ceremonies and ostentatious ritual, is the most delusive. Let us attach more importance to deeds than to creeds. The only things which can follow us beyond the grave are our actions. Our passports to immortality will con- tain no references to the church or sect we belong to. To believe otherwise, surely indicates a small and piti- able conception of Divine justice.—Yours &c., REFORMER.

- - - - A labour camp has been formed on a farm a short distance from Yarmouth. Mr. Fletcher Dodd, who has taken the farmhouse for the summer months, has pro- vided fifty bell tents, which are now being occupied by .several families from carious parts of the country, who are enjoying the opportunity of spending so pleasant and novel a holiday. Among those in camp are Mr. G. H. Roberts, M.P. for Norwich, and his wife and

Mr. Laurence Bolton, one of the borough auditors, has taken the public into his confidence by issuing an outspoken criticism of some of the Corporation accounts. We print his report in another column,and congratulate him on having boldly indicated what he considers are instances of the improper. spending of moneys and bad administration. The statements from such a source that over £40,000 has been spent with- out the Local Government Board sanctions, and that committees have departed from the strict terms of agreements, to the ratepayers' loss,will create a sensa- tion among the townspeople.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

The works competition in the first year of its exist- ence has been a pronounced success, and in future years will probably take a place at the head of the local cricket programme. Throughout the greatest interest has been taken in the proceedings and on Saturday a crowd assembled on the Warrington Cricket Ground to witness the final which was probably larger than any which has previously gathered on the Arpley enclosure. The conditions of the match were in themselves suffi- cient to create interest, as hard hitting—the delight of the spectators—was at a distinct premium with a cor- respondingly low value set upon stone walling. Moreover the fact that in addition to having a trial between teams which had shown themselves to be the pick of works organizations, the match was calculated to have a sporting finish, added considerably to the number of spectators. The supporters of the finalists, P. and K. and Walkers, were strongly in evidence and factional enthusiasm added interest to the proceedings.

Walkers won the toss and their captain was perhaps guilty of an error of judgment in putting his opponents in on a wicket which was on the slow side. Of course there was the prospect of the pitch improving 93 the afternoon proceeded but the wicket was never really difficult and the advantage of having first knock could not be gainsaid. Thompson and Gough opened the innings against the deliveries of Dargan and Norman, and the start was not inspiring. True the batsmen defended their wickets well, but five runs in ten minutes when scoring against time, was not over-encouraging. Thompson, however, warmed to his work and indulged in some free hitting taking six off two balls from Dargan. Dargan however had his revenge as he accepted a chance which Thompson gave him off Norman's bowling. Gough and Tarbuck did little. The last named when he had made two was ont lbw to Dargan, whilst Gough was caught in the long field. Lightdid not remain long at the wicket. The first ball from Norman he urged in the direction of cover point. The second he missed altogether and the three succeeding deliveries he also failed to play. The last ball of the over also beat him but this time Norman found his length and upset the wickets.

Matters were not exactly going on in a pleasing way for P. and K. when Bennett and Partridge were associa- ted. Bennett at once showed a disposition to hit, and his example being followed by Partridge the score steadily rose. Dargan was losing his effectiveness which he sacrificed for the sake of speed. He could not have made a greater mistake, as slower and more tricky bowling would have done more damage. The batsmen were not slow to appreciate Dargan's falling off, and punished him pretty severely. In fact, they became a little venturesome, and in attempting to steal a run Bennett was easily put out. Appleton drove Norman bard over the bowler's head, but Baird running in brought off a splendid catch. Bunch sent up tbe fifty by a single off Dargan, and immediately lost Partridge' who lifted the ball whilst trying to pull Dargan. Bunch meant business, but his stay was short, as when he was six he ran himself out. Gardener after a single pulled Norman to the leg for four, and with the next ball was clean bowled, and the 50 minutes being up the innings closed for GI

Walker's started ingloriously, Dargan and Ashton walked to the wickets with confidence but were unable to do anything with the bowling of Bennett who in his first over dismissed Ashton. Dugan only placed one to his credit before Thompson found his stumps. Thompson was bowling unusually well and had hard lines in not getting Milner's wicket, Gough missing a very easy catch. The mistake however, was not eYpen- sive as Milner a few balls later returned hard to the bowler who tipped the leather into the air and held it at the second attempt. A splendid return by Tarbuck resulted in Baird's dismissal and Walker's had lost four wickets for 11 run 3. The score was carried to 32 for five when Pearson and Norman were together. Thompson sent down some tempting balls to Pearson but, the batsman was careful. Patience was however rewarded as at least Thompson induced Pearson to hit out with the result that he lost his wicket-34 for 7.

Malloy barely reached the wicket before he had to return as Thompson found his stumps with his first ball —3l for S. It appeared as though P. and K. were to win easily but Walkers did not give up hope and Darton commenced to bang the bowling about. He was playing with confidence and was halting against time. Walker's supporters were jubilant. They would win after all if Darton could keep up his hitting. But they had reckoned without Thompson and Bennet who sent down deliveries which required to be played with the greatest care and Darton had to restrain his eagerness to score. Walker's supporters were on tenter hooks. Their team required eleven rims to win and had only a few minutes to bat. Thompson ventured to pause for a moment to place his field and was greeted with cries of" Go on -bowling." Thompson went on bowling and kis over was the last as time intervened and Walker' had to retire beaten by four runs.

After the match the medals—gold for the winners and silver for the runners-up—wero presented by Mr. R. T. Fairclough. Gold medals were also presented to J. Duckworth for the highest individual score 05 not out) and to J. Ward for the best bowling perform- ance (five wickets for one run).

Crosfields met Lostock Gralam at Hood-lane on Satur- day. Lostock won the toss and batted first compiling 70 runs. The home team, who had not full strength out, made but a moderate show in reply, being dismissed for 37 runs, H. Ford scoring 21 of the total. Mawds- ley's "slows " accounted for six of the wickets.

Warrington visited Wigan and for the second time this season were victorious over the local eleven. The outstanding feature of the Warrington innings was a brilliant display by W. Richardson who carried out his bat after making 56 without a single faulty stroke. He has found his best form at last! The fielding of the visitors was also exceptionally smart while Connor and Creswell bowled with deadly effect. The Warring- tonians are certainly to be congratulated on trouncing their opponents by a 73 majority.

Heavy scoring characterized Warrington 2nd,s encounter with Bolton 2nd which ended in a draw. The Warrington innings realized 203, the highest scorer being S. Baxter whose 59 included ten fours. R. Pierpoint made an excellent 44 and Sergeant Knight ran up 23. Bolton had responded with 146 for the loss of three wickets when the time limit expired. H. P. Paeey was in grand form and knocked up 77 which included one six and twelve fours.
Penketh gained a victory over Prescott's team while Grappenhall triumphed over Hough Green. St. Paul's visited Stretton and were defeated by the margin of 16.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

The bowling section of the Crosfleld Recreation Club on Saturday accepted an invitation from the Garswood Hall Colliery Recreation Club to a game of bowls, and paid a visit to the well-laid-out recreation ground at Bryn. The colliery institute club possesses three fine greens. The Soapery players got together a fair team of bowlers, and considering this is their first season, are to be congratulated upon making such a good fight against their powerful opponents. Several well-con- tested games took place, although the soapmen were at sea on the long lengths and the match concluded in a win for the home team by 42G to 243. After the game both teams sat down to a substantial knife-and-fork tea, provided by the home team in the institute. During the repast a musical programme was gone through by the Garswood Male Voice Choir, under the conductor- ship of Mr. Morris, which added to the enjoyment of the proceedings.

To all appearances the programme of the Warrington Works Bowling League is going to encroach upon the football season and this is due not so much to the number of events to be decided as to the laxity of tho responsiblecommittee. To begin with the number of competing clubs showed a considerable increase upon any previous season, and again it was decided to run a consolation competition in connection with the tourna- ment. In both of these matters the committee is to be congratulated but they are open to criticism in not having made special arrangements to cope with the extra amount of play which they involve. With a laudable desire to assist the clubs they have practically allowed the various teams to fix their own dates an having done this much the least that could have been expected of them was that they would have insisted that.fixtureq. once arranged, must be completed. Instead of doing this they have allowed a further re-arrangement with the result that they are at present behind in their work. On Saturday for instance several of the clubs in the competition found it inconvenient to place a team on the green. Instead of any penalty being attached their games were adjourned with the result that whilst Saturday's programme was incomplete, delay will be occasioned in the later stages while these teams decide their games. It is to be hoped that in future the committee will rule matters with a firmer hand, and without being unduly harsh,will insist that on or before a certain date all arranged matches shall be decided.

In the fourth round of the competition proper on Saturday Rylands (No. 1) secured an easy victory ovef Whitecross (No. 2). The match was practically won in the opening stages as Rylands started on their venture with surprising success. A. Shaw and J. Millman were the first to be associated and Shaw succeeded in clean plating his man, winning in nine ends. W.Roughly was almost equally prominent and won 15-I,Rylands thereby having a lead of 2D points as the result of the past two years. The remaining men played up with confidence and whilst they met with temporary reverses their star was ever in the ascendant and in the end they won by a 1 handsome margin.

The second round was productive of more excitement, as the two games which were decided were won by the smallest possible number of points. Playing against Itylands (No. 2), Greenings opened well, Welsby

The closing gams was naturally followed very closely. The players were Newton and Straw and the Ryland's man started off with two singles and then went to 4-1. The nest end went to Straw ani a double to the same player brought the scores level. Straw had found his length and from fonr all ran to 13-5 and then to 14-6. It appeared at this stage as though the result was a foregone conclusion but Newton asserted himself and carried his score to eleven. His side then required one point to make a tie and two to claim the match but Straw got hi % first wood home arid Greenings qualified for the third round.

Rylands (No 3) started well in their match with Orford Tannery, and on the first game secured a lead of ten points, Int the lead was not maintained. They commenced to go down when Stringer and Meakin were on the green, the Orford man playing a superior game, and winning 15-10, Apparently Rylands had struck a vein of ill-luck, as their next two men also lost, and

Orford were given a lead of two points. It was at this stage, so to speak, that the fun commenced Jolley played up well, and in his match with Skelhorn was always master of the situation, and winning 15-6 Rylands again went to the front this time by seven points. In fact, when Spencer and Cunningham took the green they had almost begun to congratulate themselves upon having achieved a victory. Never, however, was the old saw about them having many a slip better illustrated. The Orford man was irrestible, and running from .1-1 to 11-2 and then to 15-6 the Tannery qualified for the third round by two points.

Again to-day the competition programme is tem- porarily suspended a match having been arranged between the Warrington Works League and the Eccles Borough Workshops Association. The match will be played on the bowling green attached to the Bowling Green Inn and the proceeds will be devoted to charity, , half going to the Warrington Nursing Association and half to the St. Joseph's Homes, Patricroft. The War- rington team will be led by the old veteran player George Ball and will consist of G. Ball, jun., W. Ellison, El. Daintith, W. Simister' J. Houghton, S. Massey, G. Holbrook, A. Gleave, B. Tomlinson, J. Harrison, J. Bowyer, W. Andrews, J. Roberts, and W. Patrick ; reserves, A. Crosland. T. Lawton, J. Flutchinson, P. Hankinson, J. Firth, G. Clive ; referee, N. Cook. Play will commence at 2 o'clock.

Warrington Cemetery players have every reason to remember Leigh Railway, and the memory will not be sweet. In the Lancashire and Cheshire County Com- petition the first team were riding triumphantly to victory until they came a cropper over the Leigh hurdle. In the second team competition the local men qualified for the final only to meet and be defelted by the Railway moo. It is rumoured that in the Cemetery camp there are certain dark rautterings to the effect that next year they will have revenge—a swift and certain It-r-evenge.

The Prince of Wales aldfellows are noted for their keeness in the direction of advancing the interest of the Lodge and they have also gained a reputation for enthusiasm on the bowling green. Their interest was firstaroused by the presentation of a cup for competi- tion, by Bro. A. H. Crosfleld, M.P., and the annual tournament for the cup and other prizes, attracts a lare entry. This year's programme was completed on Saturday over the Sankey Chapel House green and resulted in an enjoyable afternoon's play. The past holders of the cup, Bros. Freeman and Middleton were defeated in the first round, the trophy falling to Bro. T. Bolton who in the final defeated R. Cook 13-8. The entries for the main open to all Oddfellovvs in the Warrington district close to-day and there is every prospect of a record cempetition. If enthusiasm on the part of the officials will bring succe.s, then success is assured.

Swimming. Warrington entertained Port Sunlight in a friendly encounter, at the Leigh-street baths on Thursday even- ing. In the first half the home team defended the deep end and Port Sunlight at once attacked but their shoot- ing was faulty and lacked the necessary sting. C. Ashton put in some long shots, and his brother had a splendid opening which, however, he spoiled by sending the leather over the bar. Pemberton next netted the ball, but the point was not allowed.

In the second half Warrington completely witplayed the visitors and Sutton opened the scoring. From this stage Praguell was given a great deal of work to do and was beaten four times the scorers being Ashton (2), Sutton (1) and Pemberton (1), whilst Port Sunlight only once succeeded in getting past Woods.
Prior to the match the teams indulgeel in a squadron race which was won by Port Sunlight by a yard.

A junior handicap was also decided on Thursday even- ing in which the heat winners were T. Tanner (goes at 6), W Jolley (3), H. Harding (7), and H. Beaman (7). In the final Tanner swam well and won by a foot. Harding was second with Jolly third.

The semi-final for the works squadron race will be held on September 6th, when Warrington will also meet Wigan in connection with the Liverpool and District League. The finalists are Fletcher's v. P. and K. and Monks Hall v. Corporation.

Mr. John Fairhurst (the Borough Treasurer) has this week issued the annual abstract of the accounts of the Corporation of Warrington for the year ended 31st March 1900. The volume this year exceeds 200 pages and will provide the inquiring ratepayer with ample material for study. The liabilities of the borough amount to £1,233,253 17s. 9d. and the assets to £1,02,807 18s. 3id. leaving a balance on the credit side of .+:429,003 Os. 61d. Owing to pressure on our space we are unable to give a detailed summary of the accounts.

LAURENCE BOLTON'S REPORT. Mr. Laurence Bolton, one of the elective auditors for the borough, has handed to 113 for publication the following signed rep-tit oa the votr's ac.t Ja its "I have this day together with one of my co-auditors, signed a formal certificate. as to . the

arithmetical ac-curacy of the accounts under review. I now wish to draw the attention of the rate- payers to the following items. With regard to the accounts of the Water Department a claim dated 25th May, 1935 still remains to be settled which ma i materially add to the capital figure now shown in the accounts of that department, and a sum of £274 3s. Bd. for report, etc., re a contract, which in my opinion shauld have been included in the same section of the accounts, has been charged against the Borough Rate Revenue Account. No Local Government Board sanction has been obtained in reference to the expenditure of £31,204 15s. on Street Improvements and £107988 is. on the Water Account. The Corporation subscribes to various institutions and societies to the extent of upwards of £5O per annum. ,

A sum of .-ClO2 15s. 91.7 is charged against the Borough Rate Revenue Account for Library purposes in addition to the usual 11d. rate. The giddleton Scholarship Fund is still being allowed to accumulate instead of being disbursed in accordance with the terms of the bequest. In at least two instances the terms of agreements made by the Corporation have not been strictly adhered to by the cmamittees concerned, to the ratepayers' loss. I shall be pleased to answer any questions from interested ratepayers with regard to the accounts of the Corporation so far as it lies in my power. LAURENCE BOLTON. 17th August, 1006.

div.head: CROSFIELDS' BAND AT CALAIS.
div.p: CROSFIELDS' BAND AT CALAIS.
A WONDERFUL RECEPTION. Continuous Round of Pleasure.

On Thursday night Crosfield's band returned from Calais after haying for several days been the guests of the French town. The visit was the outcome of an invitation from the Mayor of Calais to join in the great annual fete. They left Warrington on Saturday at midnight, having earlier in the day given a per- formance in the Park in aid of the Infirmary extension fund. They received a royal welcome on arrival at their destination, the pier which forms the Calais harbour being thronged with a dense, cheering crowd.l When they struck up the 'Marsellaise the enthu- siasm was increased and was followed with criesl of " The King, the King!" The band responded with the National Anthem and the Frenchmen I respectfully took off their hats. It was an evidence of the sincerity of the entente cordiale that the same attitude was noticed every time the National Anthem was struck up. When the bat drew alongside the pier the band were welcomed by the British Consul, and Mr. Leon Vincent, president of the fete, and the fête committee. The band formed up and marched to their quarters, the Hotel du Commerce, the route being thickly lined with a delighted crowd, who heartily cheered their playing of a spirited march. In the evening they proceeded to the Town Hall, where they were received by the Mayor and Corporation who welcomed them in the name of Calais whose guests he informed them they were. The Casino and every place, of entertainment was thrown open to them their 'uniforms being a sufficient passport, to to ensure free admittance. In the evening they aave a concert on the promenade, and it was expressive of the enthusiam which their visit aroused that throughout their stay every selection:which they gave was encored, some having to be rendered three or four times. On Monday they visited the largest and most up-to-date lace factory in the town. In the evening at a banquet atten,ded by deputations and officials, Mr. Mosse was given A place of honour opposite La Reine des Halles (queen of the Parisian markets, a lady whose beauty entitles her to election to the position.) The band performed on the terrace of the Town Hall being listened to by a huge crowd. On Tuesday a biscuit factory was visited and in the evening a con- cert was given in the public gardens which , were splendidly illuminated for the occasion, the crowd greeting their efforts with cries of "Tipping." Wednesday was a national holiday and the band was given the post of honour at the head of the procession. At the close of the proceedings they marched to the Town Hall when the Mayor, on behalf of the President of the Republic, presented Mr.Mosse with a handsome s6vres vase. In the evening a grand ball was given in their honour at which the men had a splendid time. At the ball a rather amusing butl expressive incident occurred. Mr. Moss was intro- duced to the "Mother of the markets" no aged dame with whom he danced. The old lady was wildly enthusiastic and the couple had the floor to them- selves, the other dancers gathering round in a circle. All of a sudden the old lady ceased dancing and throwing her arms round Mr. Mosse's neck kissed him several times, much to the delight of the onlookers. The return journey was commenced at 12.30 the band being accorded a remarkable ovation as they left for the pier. Warrington was reached at midnight, the men being welcomed back by Dr. and Miss Markel. To use Arr. Mosse'a words "they were immensely pleased with their reception and had a really wonderful time."
