div.head: WARRINGTON SHOW. SUCCESS MARRED BY RAIN. A Creditable Exhibition.
div.p: WARRINGTON SHOW. SUCCESS MARRED BY RAIN. A Creditable Exhibition.

The weather was indeed unkind to those who had worked so hard for the success of the Warrington , Show which took place in Walton Park on Thursday When the day broke the outlook was threatening and there was no improvement as time wore on. True there were fiftful gleams of sunshine, but often dark clouds gathered and exceedingly heavy rain caused all to beat a retreat to the nearest place of shelter and saturated the show ground. OE course the con- ditions were a serious drawback to success from a numerical and financial standpoint. Of those good people from various parts of Lancashire and Cheshire to whom agriculture is the most absorbing of pursuits there was a large muster. Where the attendance suffered was in the decreased patronage of residents of Warrington and district who usually visit the show not so much to take a keen interest in the exhibits as to enjoy a pleasant afternoon amid the picuresque surroundings of Walton Park. And here the indebtedness of the Society to the President, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., must once more be noted. Every year he willingly places his extensive grounds at the disposal of the Society and a more suitable spot for the show it would be impossible to find. On all sides the outlook is delightful, the wealth of trees and the undulating fields making a pretty picture. Then the beautiful gardens and the well-kept stables and piggeries are thrown open for inspection and this con- cession is always highly appreciated. Thursday's unpropitious weather was the more to be regretted because the show itself was certainly the best which the Society has ever organized. It would undoubtedly take front rank in the one day shows of the kingdom. The entries, which numbered 460, created a record and in many sections the competition was remark- ably keen. The show is pre-eminently one for horses and this year there was a magnificent display of shires. Hunters and hackneys also were in large numbers, but the harness classes showed a decline. The exhibits of cattle and produce, while not numeri- cally strong, were very creditable. A new departure —and a commendable one too—was the holding of a horticultural show confined to the Walton district. The venture was taken up with enthusiasm and the show formed one of the most attractive features, the arrangement of the choice flowers and fruit which were displayed being very pleasing. ' During the day there was steady stream of vehicles 1 ' conveying visitors to the Park, and an innovation by the Warrington Motor Carriage Company in the shape] of a motor waggonette which plied to and from town at regular intervals,met with popular favour. All who visited the show derived a great deal of pleasure from listening to the splendid programme of music submitted by the well-known Yorkshire Hussars' Band,under the conductorship of Mr.S.Cramer Suckley. The band is deservedly one of the most popular which visits this district, and selections of the irtost varied character were given with a taste and expressioa which called forth the highest enlogiums. A special word of praise is due to Ser,c,,t J.Paley,whose cornet solos were most artistically played. The arangements for the show were in every way admirable, the Society being fortunate in having an excellent band of officials. '"Alr. H. Beresford Melville is an indefatigable hon. secretary, and to him in a great measure is due the fact that the show passed off without the slightest bitch. SOME FEATURES OF THE SHOW.

First a—n-21 foremost was the ;ire- -1;;;;;;cti-on which would hold its own with any one day show in the country. While the two year old filly classes were rather weak, the brood mares and foals were the best over seen at Walton. Some idea of the merit of the class is given by the fact that the first prize brood mare at Lytham the previous day could only stand fourth. As usual Mr. James Gould, of Lymm was the principal winner—in fact he carried everything before him, securing the first prize in every open class. The Dis- trict Championship Cup went to Lymm Blossom a notable winner which secured the third prize at London this year, and the second las& year. first at Shropshire and West Midland Show,the three firsts and a champion- ship at Birkenhead and second at the Royal Lancashire. Lymru Bloom which was reserve for tho cup and first in her class won three firsts and a fifty guinea cup at Birkenhead and second at the Royal Lancashire. Messrs. Ainscough's handsome chestnut Ambrosia was third in the brood iflare class. There were a dozen colts, and Mr. Gould's winner by Raithby Tom was second at Birkenhead, where he might well have won. Filly foals were a strong class and one of the best in the section. Here the final battle was between Mr. Gould's Lynirn Starlight, by itaithby Tom, and Mr. Willaston Queen, by Mr. J. W. Kenworthy's , Matchless Waiter. The judges disazreed, and Mr.Bain- brid.,,,e, called in as referee, gave the palm to Mr. Gould's filly. Mr. Allen's was first foal at Birkenhead. while Mr. Gould's filly was fourth and his colt second. , Good foals by Ambush and Matchless Waiter followed. The district classes of mares and foals followed the same order, save that first prize-winners cannot now compete again. There were only four district yearling colts, and in fillies Mr. Gould's sturdy Grey Queen, by , Lynim Lion, first at Birkenhead and Lancaster, won again. A heavy active filly by Ambush won in two year ' olds.

In the hunter section. the brood mares, yearling and two-year-olds were not above the average, but the novice class was excellent. -Al r. Drage's winner is a tremendous goer, and a nice ride withal. Mr. Gale was second with another galloper with beautiful manners, land Mr. F. B. Wilkinson's third is also a good mover, 1 but lacks the size of the others. Mr. Geoffrey Kenyon's chestnut, "The Swell," a winner at Edgworth and elsewhere locally, stood well up. The next novice class had to be up to over 14st. 71b., and three good hunters were at the top, but Mr. Stokes led well The open class, to carry 13st. and not over 14st. 71b., was the leading class and the first four were beautiful horses. Mr. Stokes's "Wrangler " won on his going, though he gave little away to Mr. Drage's brown whose hocks, however, were not quite as good. The third award went to a good blooded horse of Mr. Gale's, and as showing the general excellence of the class, it is interesting to note that Mr. A. J. Brown's horse, which secured a championship at Peterborough last year, only I came in fourth. In the heavyweights, the famous

"Whiskey," champion everywnere this year, galloped home nicely, but his stable companion " Madrid" could only get fourth. The breeding classes of hackneys, were, comparatively speaking, better than those of hunters. Mr. Makeague, , of Newton, was a prominent winner his bright chestnut " Luvina," which was first in the brood mare class being one of the Rosador prize-winning group at the Hackney Society's Show. Foals numbered seventeen, and were one of the sights of the show. Mr. Makeagne's winner is a filly by" Blaze D..," and has never been shown before. Mr. Makeague had rather an easy win in the yearling class with a bay colt by " Blaze II.," a line natural mover that requires a little more handling to make it bad to beat. In pony brood mares Mr. Makeague's brown by" Sir Horace "had little trouble, and her foal, one of the best movers seen at its age, scored a good win. The judges were : Hunters : J. M. Richardson, Oakham : W. G. Lambarde,H.F.H. Sevenoaks. Hackney and Harness: Hon. Fredk. Wrench, Killacoona ; C. NI. E. Cooke, Baldock. Shires: R. C. Cooper, Waltham ; Henry Mackereth, Kerby Lonsdale. Butter and Cheese: Thomas Welsby, Rhyl.

THE LUNCHEON. At noon Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., entertained a large company at luncheon. Afterwards, there was a little speech making. The toast of " The Ring " was enthusiastically honoured on the proposition of the President.

Mr. J. W. Kenwortlay (Kelsall) proposed" Success to the Warrington Agricultural Society,' coupling with it the name of the President. The Society was one which as a rule had the cream of exhibits and in Sir Gilbert Greenall they had a president of whom any society in the Kingdom would be proud. (Applause.). The toast wat very cordially honoured. In responding, the President said that day was always one of great pleasure to him and he was delighted to I see the visitors and to be able to entertain them. The show had grown from very small beginnings, as those who remembered the early shows in the old Barrack yard could testify. Now they could say with truth that they had one of the best one-day shows in England. (Applause.) It was always a pleasure to him to do any- thing for the Society. They had the support of the exhibitors, and the Council would leave nothing undone to ensure that the show would be a success every year. He hoped that in future they would be favoured with better weather, as of late years the Society had been rather unfortunate in that respect. THE OFFICIALS. The principal officials, to whom every credit is due for the excellence of the arrangements, were :—Presi- dent, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart. ; Vice-President, Mr. Frank Tinsley ; Hon. Treasurer, Mr. Alfred Broome ; Secretary, Mr! H. Beresford Melville.

LATCHFORD. A LEAP OF THIRTY FEET INTO THE Ship CANAL. Sueetators' Callous Indifference. Remarkable evidence was given at an inquest which Latchford, widow of # t was held at the Dog and Dart Inn, on Thursday, on the body of Frederick Owen (40), range fitter, employed by Messrs. Richmonds, whocommiiitte lenedbescuainaciedecoonny about three weeks ago when it was decided by drowning himself in the Manchester Ship Canal, at - Latchford. Mr. Yates, district coroner, conducted the inquiry Nt which Captain Waring was present on behalf of the e r rheumatic ShipB a h t her Canal Company. fever. On Tuesday morning wileu got up he complained of being ill and of pains in t.t.o head. He drank some soda water but this made 111111 sick, probably owing to the fact that the previous night he had come home drunk. He said he would go for 5 walk and look for work and knowing be was not fit to work witness laughed at him, when he turned round and said "you will not laugh long." He took a pair of • slippers out with him and witness gave him is. She had SiliCO learnt that be pawned his boots. Her husband had been very depressed since his illness and would sit for hours with his hand to his head without speaking. She was afraid of him as he had threatened to _murder her.

r --lie;:b-J-t -Percival, 131, Knutsford-road, said that for the -past two months he had been off work owing to an accident. On Tuesday morning he met Owen in a casual manner on Warrington Bridge and asked him where he was going. Deceased replied : For a walk," and witness went with him in the direction of Stockton Heath. They called at three public-houses, deceased having two glasses of beer and a glass of whisky. While on their way they met a man named Jack Mitchell to whom deceased said, ",lack, there will be a vacancy for you shortly at Richmond's." Mitchell asked him what he' meant and Owen replied with an oath : "There will be a vacancy right enough." They had reached the corner of Fairfield-road, Stockton Heath, when the deeeased, handing witness a coin, said" Here is sixpence for you. Get out of my sight." Witness told Owen not to be foolish and handed back the money when deceased replied "If yon do not leave me I will put you over the railings into the canal." As he could not swim witness, went to give the alarm. The two young men to whom: he spoke walked to the canal side and looked into OM water and then proceeded to the cantilever bridge where they stood and watched Owen drown. (The Coroner : " That is terrible.") A man came across the road anct got a rope and a prop but they were not able to rescDj Owen. A Young man named lßowcock came up on ft bicycle and saying " I am a good swimmer "volunteered to go in after the deceased. Bowcock was lowered to the water and succeeded in getting the deceased out. When walking along Fairfield-road deceased said he had had 30s. given to him in which to go into a convalescent home. This money he said be had spent in having a jolly good time adding ".1 am not going to the home. lam going to along home." Deceased was drunk at thc time he jumped into the canal. Samuel Worrall, Great Budworth,said he saw Percival and deceased arguing in Fairfield-road. Perci appeared to be advising the deceased not to do some- thing. Percival then crossed the roadway and deceased jumped into the canal. The two young men of who: Percival spoke were only about ten yards away frot the deceased when he climbed over the railings, ant both walked on to the cantilever bridge. He went UP to Percival who tried to make out that deceased was a perfect stranger. Witness's brother went for assistance to the Stockton Heath swing bridge and returned with a life belt. They tried to reach Owen with a rope, when Bowcock came up and went into the canal after him. Deceased was quite dead when he was taken oat of the water. Harry Bowcock, 17, Stafford-road, Warrington, spe" to rescuing the deceased. He was lowered to within eight feet of the water and then jumped off the roPe; Deceased was on the top of the water with his hetef underneath. He raised Owen's head and noticed thsb he was then alive but unconscious. Owing to the steer bank they could not get him out of the water ad that spot and he had to be put back into the canal 0 s dragged about thirty yards. He was dead when he vrtli taken out. There was a bruise at the back of his hea as though he had caught a rock in falling. Mr. Yates to Bowcock : I think you deserve_trhy.e: ' greatest praise for your conduct. You are a v plucky man indeed. Continuing, he reviewed _et!): evidence and said he thought no importance WaS to' the , attached to Percival's denial of any knowledge, et the. deceased. He was evidently in a " blue bunk " . time. of The jury returned a verdict of" Suicide whilst unsound mind."

THE EXAMINER. AUGUST 18th 1906.

Warrington possesses an up to-date electrical work . and a large number of members of the Town Council 'found pleasure in inspecting the establishment at the close of last Friday's Council meeting. The feature which attracted most attention was the new high ten- sion plant which has just been installed and the much- -talked-of mechanical stokers. If all works chimneys ,sent forth as little smoke as the one at the electrical station we should hear very little of " the smoke nuisance." * * A bit more of Sankey-street is to be paved when the sanction of the Local Government Board has been obtained. The bit selected is opposite the late Miss Garven's premises, but why the Corporation should do such an urgent job in peacemeal fashion is a puzzle -to the ratepayers. The lower portion of the street which contains the decayed remnants of one-time wood-blocks is, without the slightest exaggeration, positive danger to vehicular traffic. Many of the holes are half a foot deep, and if nothing is done before autumn the throughfare will become impassable to all vehicle-users but the trick cyclists. * * We note that two local motorists have been 'fined for exceeding the legal speed limit on the Chester- road between Walton and Preston Brook. The efficacy of the police trap is evidently unquestionable, but the zeal of the officers is somewhat excessive. If the offenders were only doing 26 or 27 miles an hour they were committing merely a technical offence which might have been winked at without any serious depar- ture from the path of police duty. Motoring at these speeds on an open country road is less menacing to the public safety than is the average cab or 'bus in the town. Commonsense as well as law is required in the admintstration of justice, a fact which police and magistrates occasionally forget. * There are thousands of people in Warrington who dill heartily wish " God speed "to Nurse Whitfield, .N"urse Jacocks and Nurse Leshaw on their departure from the town. They have for several years rendered magnificent service to the poor and afflicted, with a devotion to duty and a disregard of personal comfort which have won for them the ungrudging admiration of all, The presentationsmade on Monday evening are a small testimony of the public esteem, and we hope they will lighten the hearts of these ladies in the unhappy circumstances of their departure. The pre- judices which have brought about the resignations are typical of certain classes in Warrington, but we hope the nurses will realise that there is a very warm regard for themselves and their work in the hearts of the great majority of Warrington people.

A Popular Tour. ba its recent summer number 'Cycling' published a series of twenty-nine attractive tours, furnished on post-cards by readers, and asked the public to select the best six. As a result of this plebiscite an order of men was arrived at, and it is of interest to note thirthe tour which secured premier position was "London to the Peak District," an eight days cycling itinerary embracing the follow- ing places: Hitchin (detour to Garden City), Bedford, Leicester, Derby, Matlock (caves), Bake- well (Haddon Hall), Buxton, Knutsford (Totten Park), Northwich (salt mines), Chester, Shrewsbury, Worcester (cathedral), Tewkesbury (abbey), and Oxford. The total 'distance is 442 miles, or an average of 55 miles a day. The other five districts which won most votes respectively were West of England, Devon, Hampshire, and the Isle of Wight, Shakespeare's Country, and Scotland. Cycle Camper's Light Outfit. It is not surprising to find that the votaries of r, cycle camping are discovering. the desirability of cutting down the weight of their equipment to the smallest possible point compatible with efficiency. In the circular of the Association of Campers, 4 25 lb. is given as the weight of a single camper's ,tfit, or 30-351 h for two persons. Mr. 0. G. " illiams, in the • Irish Cyclist, describes an outfit he has assembled which treighs 13 lb. single, or 20 lb. double. This includes a Primus stove, and if a ,Sirram pad stove were substituted there would be aAaving of 2 lb. Mr. Williams's outfit includes all the usual essentials, but his utensils are all Of aluminium, and he manages to dispense .with carriers, which sometimes weigh over 71h. alone. The Japanese basket in which the outfit is packed, is secured crosswise by straps to the back stays of the machine. Mr. Williams's complete kit, includ- ing bis bicycle, only weights 43 lb. Of course, ideas vary as to the irreducible minimum of articles to be carried; Mr. Mecredy, for example, being content with an equipment which only weighs just ever 12 lb. for two persons. s The Rule of the Road. ° It is surprising that misconception should exist in the minds of certain magistrates as regards the legal existence of • the rule of the road. More \than once the statement has been made from the Bench that there was no such thing as a rule of the road, but merely custom. This is not the case, for, as a veteran cyclist has lately pointed out, the Highway Act of 1835, section 78, imposes a considerable penalty on the driver of a carriage who does note keep to the left when meeting another carriage. Moreover, the provisions of this Act are to be found in Archibald's Police Guide '—a digest of. the Principal Acts of Parliament anent matters .with Which the police are concerned—this work being kept for reference in every police-station. It is therefore plain that no motorist, cyclist, nor' car- riage driver can violate the rule of the road, with intention to obstruct others, without rendering himself liable to a conviction under this Act, if a summers be obtained against him. And the police Should be aware of this. Strange Taring Grounds. ' Enthusiasm is a quality that grows by what it feeds on. The cycling tourist sometimes becomes on ~unconscious enthusiast, and his adventurous wanderings awheel are apt to astonish the every- day rider. To explore country not hitherto travelled through by a cyclist, becomes a passion. to gratify which the enthusiastic tourist will travel -far, enduring awful roads, with wretched accent. toodation, and the solitude of the desert on reach- ing his goal. Of course, the cyclist in quest`of fine scenery must always be prepared to sacrifice something. but the average rider draws the line at risking his neck on the edges of precipices, or putting up with the poorest food and lodging at the end of each arduous day's ride. Good enough for him, as a rule, are the beaten tracks, and the hills that can be ridden down, even if they have to be walked up. Unless himself of the stuff •enthnsiasts are made of, the cyclist should resist l'eYtg hived into the natural fastnesses of remote wild districts. The Problem of Cycle Storage. 41 Although the number of persons who dwell in ats has been increasing for many years, provision IS seldom made for the convenient disposal of a bicycle. Space is usually very circumscribed, and . even if a machine be swung from the ceiling, the bugbear of carrying it up and down many stairs 'cannot be ignored. In the better-class buildings, . a cycle room is often provided in the basement, "which affords; a satisfactory solution of the diffi- ,eulty ; but where only a wooden outbuilding exists, the drawbacks of damp are usualty manifested 'during the winter months.
